name: Acadia
summary: Granite mountains rising straight from the Atlantic on Maine's Mount Desert Island, with outposts on the Schoodic Peninsula and Isle au Haut. Sunrise from Cadillac Mountain, tea at Jordan Pond and 45 miles of car-free carriage roads — the first national park east of the Mississippi.

image.caption: Entrance Fee Required Year-Round
image.altText: Two small, booth-like buildings are positioned across a roadway. Park rangers are seated at open win

name: National Park of American Samoa
summary: The only US national park south of the equator: rainforest ridges, coral reefs and white-sand beaches on three Samoan islands. The land is leased from village councils, and the park protects the Samoan way of life alongside the reef and the fruit bats.

image.caption: Back side of Pola Island from Tuafanua Trail
image.altText: Tuafanua Trail

name: Arches
summary: More than two thousand natural stone arches — the densest collection anywhere — with fins, pinnacles and balanced rocks, in the red-rock desert five miles north of Moab. A bed of salt buried deep beneath the park is what made them.

image.caption: Double O Arch
image.altText: a broad, red arch with rock pinnacles in the background

name: Badlands
summary: Sharply eroded buttes and pinnacles banded in tan, red and yellow, set in the largest undisturbed mixed-grass prairie in the United States. The rock holds one of the world's richest beds of mammal fossils; bison, bighorn sheep and black-footed ferrets live on the grass above it.

image.caption: Badlands Storm
image.altText: Layered badlands formations behind fields of green grass under cloudy and billowing clouds.

name: Big Bend
summary: Where the Rio Grande turns its great bend, three worlds in one park: river canyons cut through sheer limestone, the Chihuahuan Desert, and the Chisos Mountains rising out of the middle — the only mountain range in the country held entirely within a national park.

image.caption: Blooming Cenizo
image.altText: Blooming Cenizo

name: Biscayne
summary: A park that is ninety-five percent water: shallow bay, mangrove shoreline, the northernmost of the Florida Keys and the coral reef beyond them, in sight of downtown Miami. Most of it is reached by boat, or seen underwater.

image.caption: Snorkeling
image.altText: Coral reef with two snorkelers diving below the surface

name: Black Canyon of the Gunnison
summary: A canyon so deep and narrow that stretches of its floor get only minutes of direct sun a day. The Gunnison River has cut its way down through some of the oldest rock in North America, leaving dark, sheer walls such as the Painted Wall, the tallest cliff in Colorado.

image.caption: Black Canyon near Tomichi Point
image.altText: Black Canyon near Tomichi Point

name: Bryce Canyon
summary: Not a canyon but a row of natural amphitheaters cut into the edge of a high plateau, crowded with hoodoos — the largest concentration of them anywhere. The rim stands between 8,000 and 9,000 feet, so nights are cold and the stars are some of the clearest in the country.

image.caption: Bryce Amphitheater from Inspiration Point
image.altText: A red rock landscape and plateau forest glows with the morning sun

name: Canyonlands

facts.suggestedTime: A day for each district you visit

summary: A wilderness of canyons, mesas and spires cut by the Colorado and Green rivers, which divide it into districts no road connects: the high mesa of Island in the Sky, the banded spires of the Needles, the remote Maze, and the rivers themselves.

image.caption: Canyons in The Needles district
image.altText: Small rounded canyons with large sandstone cliffs and mountains in the background

name: Capitol Reef
summary: A hundred-mile wrinkle in the earth's crust — the Waterpocket Fold — laid open as cliffs, domes, canyons and natural bridges in south-central Utah. In the middle of it, the Fremont River waters the orchards of Fruita, a pioneer settlement whose fruit visitors can still pick in season.

image.caption: Gifford House and Pendleton Barn
image.altText: Wingate Sandstone cliffs behind historic barn and farmhouse

name: Carlsbad Caverns

facts.suggestedTime: Half a day to a day

summary: More than 119 caves under the Chihuahuan Desert, dissolved out of an ancient reef by sulfuric acid. The largest is open to walk: down through the natural entrance, or by elevator, to the Big Room, the largest cave chamber in North America.

image.caption: Hall of Giants
image.altText: Photo of Giant Dome and Twin Domes in the Big Room.

name: Channel Islands

facts.suggestedTime: A day trip to one island, or a night camping

summary: Five islands off the Southern California coast and the sea around them, isolated long enough to evolve plants and animals found nowhere else — the island fox among them. Reached only by boat or small plane, they show this coast as it was before the cities.

image.caption: Giant coreopsis on Anacapa Island
image.altText: Yellow giant coreopsis covering Anacapa Island, with the lighthouse and the sea beyond.

name: Congaree

facts.suggestedTime: Half a day to a day

summary: The largest intact old-growth bottomland hardwood forest left in the southeastern United States, eighteen miles from Columbia: a floodplain of giant loblolly pines, bald cypress and tupelo, washed through by the Congaree and Wateree rivers.

image.caption: Floodplain Forest
image.altText: A view of a bottomland/floodplain forest, with wide based cypress and tupelo trees, cypress knees

name: Crater Lake
summary: A lake of startling blue in the caldera of Mount Mazama, a volcano that collapsed in a violent eruption 7,700 years ago. At 1,949 feet it is the deepest lake in the United States, and it is filled almost entirely by rain and snow.

image.caption: Wizard Island
image.altText: A view of Crater Lake and Wizard Island

name: Cuyahoga Valley
summary: A river valley between Cleveland and Akron, protected as forests, farms, waterfalls and the towpath of the Ohio & Erie Canal. The only national park that began as a national recreation area, and one of the most visited.

image.caption: Kayakers on the Cuyahoga River
image.altText: People in bright orange kayaks paddle around a bend in a river, past green trees and a rocky shore.

name: Death Valley
summary: The hottest, driest and lowest national park: salt flats 282 feet below sea level at Badwater, dunes, badlands and canyons under mountains that keep their snow into spring. The largest national park outside Alaska.

image.caption: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes
image.altText: Low, warm light skims across pale sand dunes.

name: Denali
summary: Six million acres of wild Alaska crossed by a single road, rising from taiga forest to tundra to North America's highest peak, 20,310 feet. Grizzly bears, caribou, moose, wolves and Dall sheep range across land that has never been fenced.

image.caption: Dall Sheep
image.altText: a white colored sheep standing on a mountainside overlooking a green valley

name: Dry Tortugas

facts.suggestedTime: A day trip, or a night camping on Garden Key

summary: Seven small islands seventy miles west of Key West, reached only by boat or seaplane. Massive, unfinished Fort Jefferson fills one of them; around them lie clear water, seagrass and the least disturbed coral reefs in the Florida Keys.

image.caption: Night sky at the Dry Tortugas
image.altText: A few of the stars at night with a view of Fort Jefferson.

name: Everglades
summary: The largest subtropical wilderness in the United States: a slow river of grass, sawgrass prairie, pine rockland, cypress, mangrove and the shallow waters of Florida Bay. The first national park created to protect an ecosystem rather than scenery.

image.caption: Cypress Tree Sunrise
image.altText: A sunset creates a silhouette of a cypress tree with needle-like leaves that is shaped like an 'N'.

name: Gates of the Arctic

facts.suggestedTime: A week or more, by air taxi

summary: The northernmost national park, wholly above the Arctic Circle in Alaska's Brooks Range. There are no roads, trails or services — only wild rivers, glacier-carved valleys and caribou on their age-old migrations.

image.caption: Alatna River
image.altText: Aerial view of the Alatna River as it winds through a valley

name: Gateway Arch
summary: The smallest national park: the 630-foot stainless-steel Gateway Arch on the St. Louis riverfront, the museum beneath it, and the Old Courthouse where Dred and Harriet Scott sued for their freedom.

image.caption: Morning Light at the Gateway Arch
image.altText: looking up at the curve of the Gateway Arch against the sky

name: Glacier
summary: A million acres of the northern Rockies on the Canadian border: glacier-carved valleys and lakes, wildflower meadows, grizzly bears and mountain goats, and the Going-to-the-Sun Road over Logan Pass. Its namesake glaciers are shrinking fast.

image.caption: Grinnell Glacier from Lower Grinnell Ridge in 2016
image.altText: Grinnell Glacier from Lower Grinnell Ridge in 2016

name: Glacier Bay
summary: Tidewater glaciers, fjords and temperate rainforest in Alaska's Inside Passage, in a bay that was almost entirely ice two and a half centuries ago. Homeland of the Huna Tlingit, reached only by boat or plane.

image.caption: Cruising Glacier Bay
image.altText: Cruising Glacier Bay

name: Grand Canyon
summary: A mile deep and up to eighteen miles wide, cut by the Colorado River through nearly two billion years of rock. The South Rim is open all year; the higher, cooler North Rim lost its historic lodge to the Dragon Bravo Fire in 2025.

image.caption: Sunset from Mather Point
image.altText: At Sunset, swirling rain clouds above a vast canyon filled with colorful peaks and cliff walls.

name: Grand Teton
summary: Jagged peaks rising straight out of the sagebrush flats of Jackson Hole, with no foothills between, glacial lakes at their feet and moose, elk and bison on the valley floor. Ten miles south of Yellowstone, and joined to it by a parkway.

image.caption: The Teton Range
image.altText: Granite mountains with a cloudy blue sky and green and yellow trees and plants in the foreground

name: Great Basin
summary: One mountain range rising out of the sagebrush desert of eastern Nevada to the 13,063-foot summit of Wheeler Peak, with a small glacier, bristlecone pines thousands of years old, and Lehman Caves beneath its flank. Some of the darkest night skies in the country.

image.caption: Wheeler cirque
image.altText: blue sky with green trees in mountain cirque

name: Great Sand Dunes
summary: The tallest dunes in North America, up to 750 feet high, heaped against the Sangre de Cristo Mountains at the edge of Colorado's San Luis Valley — with a seasonal creek at their foot and forest, alpine lakes and tundra above.

image.caption: Dunes and Crestone Peaks at Sunset
image.altText: Grasslands, large dunes, and snow-capped peaks at sunset

name: Great Smoky Mountains
summary: Ancient forested mountains on the Tennessee–North Carolina line, wrapped in the blue haze that gives them their name. Wildflowers, salamanders and black bears, old farmsteads at Cades Cove and Cataloochee, no entrance fee — and more visitors than any other national park.

image.caption: Winter in the Smokies
image.altText: A clear sky with a vast snowy mountain scene.

name: Guadalupe Mountains
summary: A fossil reef from an ancient sea, lifted into the four highest peaks in Texas — Guadalupe Peak at 8,751 feet, and the sheer prow of El Capitan — above the Chihuahuan Desert. A hidden canyon of maples turns red here in autumn.

image.caption: El Capitan
image.altText: El Capitan with blooming claret cup cacti

name: Haleakalā

facts.suggestedTime: A day for the summit, another for Kīpahulu

summary: The summit of Maui's great volcano, 10,023 feet up, where people gather above the clouds to watch the sun rise over a vast crater of cinder cones — and, on the far side of the mountain, the rainforest, waterfalls and pools of the Kīpahulu coast.

image.caption: 'Ahinahina blooms in Haleakala crater
image.altText: 'Ahinahina blooms in Haleakala crater

name: Hawaiʻi Volcanoes
summary: Two of the most active volcanoes on Earth — Kīlauea and Mauna Loa — from summit to sea, where lava has added new land within living memory. In Hawaiian tradition the crater is home to Pele, and the park is a World Heritage Site.

image.caption: Lava
image.altText: Fountains of molten lava erupting from within a crater next to a whirlwind formed from the eruption.

name: Hot Springs
summary: Forty-seven hot springs on the side of a mountain in the middle of a town, and the Gilded Age bathhouses built to use them. Congress set them aside in 1832, forty years before Yellowstone, so the water could belong to everyone.

image.caption: Bathhouse Row
image.altText: Stone entrance pillars in front of a row of four bathouses

name: Indiana Dunes
summary: Fifteen miles of Lake Michigan shore between Gary and Michigan City: beaches, tall dunes, bogs, prairies and woods packed with an unusual variety of plants — and the place where the science of ecological succession began.

image.caption: Central Avenue Beach Indiana Dunes National Park
image.altText: Michigan Lake beach with green grassy dunes in the background, under a blue sky.

name: Isle Royale
summary: A roadless island wilderness in the middle of Lake Superior, reached only by ferry or floatplane and closed for the winter. Its wolves and moose have been watched by scientists since 1958, in the longest-running study of predators and prey anywhere.

image.caption: Aerial View of Belle Harbor
image.altText: Aerial View of Belle Harbor

name: Joshua Tree
summary: Where two deserts meet: the higher Mojave, home of the shaggy Joshua tree, and the lower Colorado, with its cholla and ocotillo. Between them stand piles of granite boulders that draw climbers from around the world, under dark skies two hours from Los Angeles.

image.caption: Quail Springs Area at Sunset
image.altText: The sky turns hues of pink and purple over a field of Joshua trees.

name: Katmai

facts.suggestedTime: A day trip by floatplane, or several days at Brooks Camp

summary: Volcanoes, salmon and brown bears on the Alaska Peninsula. Katmai was created to protect the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes, buried by the largest eruption of the twentieth century in 1912; it is now best known for the bears that fish for salmon at Brooks Falls.

image.caption: Salmon jumping at Brooks Falls
image.altText: salmon jumping at waterfall

name: Kenai Fjords

facts.suggestedTime: Two days: one on land, one on the water

summary: The Harding Icefield, one of the largest in the United States, and the nearly forty glaciers that pour from it toward fjords on the Gulf of Alaska. Reached by road at Exit Glacier near Seward, and by boat for the whales, sea otters and puffins of the coast.

image.caption: Northwestern Fiord
image.altText: A thin bay surrounded by mountains and ice

name: Kings Canyon
summary: A glacier-carved canyon more than a mile deep on the Kings River, a vast high-Sierra wilderness rising to the 14,248-foot North Palisade, and in Grant Grove the General Grant Tree, the nation's Christmas tree. Run together with Sequoia National Park to the south.

image.caption: Kings Canyon
image.altText: A deep canyon with a forested floor and steep granite cliffs

name: Kobuk Valley
summary: North of the Arctic Circle, a broad valley where the Kobuk River winds past the Great Kobuk Sand Dunes — the largest active dunes in the Arctic — and caribou of the Western Arctic herd cross the river as they have at Onion Portage for nine thousand years.

image.caption: Kobuk Sand Dunes
image.altText: sun setting on sand dunes

name: Lake Clark

facts.suggestedTime: A day trip by floatplane, or several days

summary: A sample of all Alaska in one park: two steaming volcanoes, glaciers, long turquoise lakes, rainforest on the Cook Inlet coast and brown bears grazing its meadows — a short flight from Anchorage, and reached by no road.

image.caption: Lake Clark
image.altText: Photo of blue sky with fluffy white clouds reflect in calm lake with mountains in the background.

name: Lassen Volcanic
summary: The southernmost volcano of the Cascades, Lassen Peak, which erupted from 1914 to 1917 — and around it every type of volcano there is, with boiling mud pots, steaming vents and meadows of wildflowers that bloom late under deep snow.

image.caption: Winter at Manzanita Lake
image.altText: A frozen lake below snow-covered trees and peak

name: Mammoth Cave
summary: The longest known cave system in the world — more than 426 miles of surveyed passages — beneath the green hills and river valleys of south-central Kentucky. People have explored it for at least five thousand years.

image.caption: Historic Entrance to Mammoth Cave
image.altText: Looking out from a large cave entrance with falling water and green trees shown over the entrance.

name: Mesa Verde
summary: Some of the best-preserved Ancestral Pueblo sites in the country — more than five thousand of them, including six hundred cliff dwellings — on a high mesa in southwest Colorado. The first national park created to protect the works of people rather than nature.

image.caption: Cliff Palace
image.altText: Large cliff dwelling in cliff alcove

name: Mount Rainier
summary: A glacier-clad volcano, 14,410 feet high, standing alone above the Cascades within sight of Seattle — the most glaciated peak in the contiguous United States, ringed by wildflower meadows and ancient forest.

image.caption: Narada Falls Rainbow
image.altText: A fan-shaped waterfall cascades over lava cliffs with a rainbow in its mist.

name: New River Gorge
summary: One of the oldest rivers on the continent, running north through a deep Appalachian gorge in West Virginia — known for whitewater, sandstone climbing walls and the steel arch of the New River Gorge Bridge, with the ruins of coal towns in the woods below.

image.caption: Horseshoe Bend from Grandview
image.altText: bend in the river

name: North Cascades
summary: Jagged peaks crowned by more than three hundred glaciers, less than three hours from Seattle — the largest glacier system in the contiguous United States, with the turquoise lakes of the Skagit River beneath it and one highway through.

image.caption: Stehekin - Looking down Lake Chelan
image.altText: boats on the water with mountains and trees surrounding

name: Olympic
summary: Nearly a million acres on Washington's Olympic Peninsula holding three parks in one: glacier-capped mountains, the moss-hung rainforests of the Hoh and Quinault valleys, and more than seventy miles of wild Pacific coast.

image.caption: Roosevelt Elk
image.altText: A herd of elk crossing a river.

name: Petrified Forest

facts.suggestedTime: Half a day to a day

summary: One of the world's largest and most colourful collections of petrified wood, scattered across the badlands of the Painted Desert in northeastern Arizona — trees that grew more than two hundred million years ago, turned to quartz. Old Route 66 crosses it.

image.caption: Petrified Forest National Wilderness Area
image.altText: Sunlit Painted Desert hills of the Petrified Forest National Wilderness Area

name: Pinnacles

facts.suggestedTime: A day for one side; two to see both

summary: Rock spires and talus caves in California's Coast Ranges — half of an ancient volcano, carried north along the San Andreas Fault. Condors ride the thermals over the High Peaks, and bats roost in the caves. Two entrances, east and west, with no road between them.

image.caption: Balconies Caves
image.altText: Boulders in the Balconies Cave.

name: Redwood
summary: The world's tallest trees, in old-growth coast redwood forest along the northern California coast, managed jointly with three state parks. Fern-walled canyons, wild beaches, Roosevelt elk and the mouth of the Klamath River.

image.caption: Fish-eye view of Redwood canopy
image.altText: View from forest floor looking straight up. Ferns as seen close up and redwood trunks meet.

name: Rocky Mountain
summary: High peaks, alpine lakes and tundra astride the Continental Divide in northern Colorado, crossed by Trail Ridge Road at over 12,000 feet. Elk in the meadows, the Colorado River's headwaters on the west side, and Longs Peak above it all.

image.caption: Cub Lake in fall
image.altText: Cub Lake with reflections. Yellow and brown grasses line the edge of the lake.

name: Saguaro

facts.suggestedTime: A day; half a day for each district

summary: Forests of giant saguaro cactus in two districts either side of Tucson, Arizona. The Tucson Mountain District is low desert with Hohokam petroglyphs; the Rincon Mountain District climbs from desert to pine forest on Mica Mountain.

image.caption: Saguaro Flowers
image.altText: Saguaro flowers

name: Sequoia
summary: The largest trees on Earth, giant sequoias in the Giant Forest, on the western slope of the southern Sierra Nevada. The park rises from oak foothills to the summit of Mount Whitney, the highest point in the contiguous United States, with marble caverns in between.

image.caption: The Tablelands
image.altText: A steep granite slope leads from forest to a bare alpine landscape

name: Shenandoah
summary: A long, narrow park on the crest of Virginia's Blue Ridge, 75 miles from Washington, D.C., followed for 105 miles by Skyline Drive. Waterfalls in wooded hollows, rocky summits, black bears, autumn colour — and the remains of the mountain communities removed to make it.

image.caption: Animal Crossing
image.altText: White-tailed bucks sparring in Big Meadows

name: Theodore Roosevelt
summary: Badlands along the Little Missouri River in western North Dakota, where a young Theodore Roosevelt ranched in the 1880s. Bison, wild horses and prairie dog towns, in three separate units — the only national park named for one person.

image.caption: River Bend Overlook, North Unit
image.altText: A colorfully striped butte in the foreground overlooks a dark green badlands landscape

name: Virgin Islands
summary: Most of the island of St. John in the US Virgin Islands — white-sand bays, coral reefs, dry tropical forest, Taíno petroglyphs and the ruins of Danish sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans. Reached by ferry from St. Thomas.

image.caption: Trunk Bay
image.altText: Turquoise water laps white sandy shore fringed with lush green vegetation.

name: Voyageurs

facts.suggestedTime: Two to three days, with time on the water

summary: A water park on the Canadian border in northern Minnesota — big lakes, thousands of islands and the roadless Kabetogama Peninsula, best explored by boat. Named for the French-Canadian voyageurs who paddled the fur-trade route through it.

image.caption: Northern Lights Over Kabetogama
image.altText: Photograph of northern lights over a lake.

name: White Sands

facts.suggestedTime: Half a day to a day

summary: The world's largest gypsum dunefield, rising from New Mexico's Tularosa Basin — waves of brilliant white sand that stay cool underfoot. Sled the dunes, walk them at sunset, and look for the ice-age footprints and pale animals found nowhere else.

image.caption: Sunset
image.altText: White dunes in foreground with sun setting behind mountain.

name: Wind Cave

facts.suggestedTime: Half a day to a day

summary: One of the longest and most complex caves in the world, beneath mixed-grass prairie and ponderosa pine in South Dakota's Black Hills. The cave holds most of the world's known boxwork; above ground, bison, elk and prairie dogs roam.

image.caption: Boxwork in the Elk's Room
image.altText: Thin fins of calcite forming box-shaped openings, called boxwork, on a cave ceiling.

name: Wrangell–St. Elias
summary: The largest national park in the United States: a wilderness of volcanoes, ice fields and glaciers in southeast Alaska, where the Wrangell, St. Elias and Chugach mountains meet. The historic Kennecott copper mill stands at its heart, at the end of a sixty-mile gravel road.

image.caption: Icy Bay with Mt. St. Elias
image.altText: Glaciers loom over the ocean with large snowy mountains rising into blue skies

name: Yellowstone
summary: The world's first national park, on a volcanic hotspot where Wyoming meets Montana and Idaho. More than half the world's geysers, Old Faithful and Grand Prismatic Spring among them, the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone, and bison, wolves and grizzly bears roaming free.

image.caption: Electric Peak Sunset
image.altText: The sun sets behind the sharp point of a snow-covered mountain; pink clouds are reflected in a pond

name: Yosemite
summary: Granite walls, waterfalls and giant sequoias in California's Sierra Nevada — Yosemite Valley, El Capitan and Half Dome, and the high country of Tuolumne Meadows beyond. Its 1864 grant was the first time the US government set land aside for preservation.

image.caption: Half Dome
image.altText: Granite dome with trace amounts of snow.

name: Zion
summary: A canyon cut half a mile deep into red and cream Navajo Sandstone by the Virgin River in southwestern Utah. Hike up the river itself in the Narrows, climb the chained ridge of Angels Landing, or drive the switchbacks and tunnel of the east side. Utah's first national park.

image.caption: The Watchman
image.altText: A triangular sandstone mountain overlooks green and yellow foliage. A cloudy blue sky is overhead.

name: Abraham Lincoln Birthplace
summary: For over a century people from around the world have come to rural Central Kentucky to honor the humble beginnings of our 16th president, Abraham Lincoln. His early life on Kentucky's frontier shaped his character and prepared him to lead the nation through Civil War. Visit our country's first memorial to Lincoln, built with donations from young and old, and the site of his childhood home.

image.caption: The Memorial Building
image.altText: The first memorial erected to honor Abraham Lincoln

name: Adams
summary: From the sweet little farm at the foot of Penn’s Hill to the gentleman’s country estate at Peace field, Adams National Historical Park is the story of “heroes, statesmen, philosophers…and learned women” whose ideas and actions helped to transform thirteen disparate colonies into one united nation.

image.caption: The John and John Quincy Adams Birthplaces
image.altText: The Birthplaces of Presidents John Adams (right) and John Quincy Adams (left)

name: African American Civil War Memorial
summary: Over 200,000 African-American soldiers and sailors served in the U.S. Army and Navy during the Civil War. Their service helped to end the war and free over four million slaves. The African American Civil War Memorial honors their service and sacrifice.

image.caption: African American Civil War Memorial
image.altText: Bronze statue of African American Civil War soldiers.

name: African Burial Ground
summary: The African Burial Ground stands as the oldest and largest known excavated burial site in North America for both free and enslaved Africans. It offers a profound testament to the enduring legacy of African communities whose labor, resilience, and cultural contributions were fundamental in shaping the development of New York.

image.caption: African Burial Ground Memorial
image.altText: African Burial Ground Memorial

name: Agate Fossil Beds
summary: In the early 1900s, paleontologists unearthed the Age of Mammals when they found full skeletons of extinct Miocene mammals in the hills of Nebraska -- species previously only known through fragments. At the same time, an age of friendship began between rancher James Cook and Chief Red Cloud of the Lakota. These two unprecedented events are preserved and protected here... at Agate Fossil Beds.

image.caption: Visitor Center on the Prairie
image.altText: The visitor center sits in the middle of mixed grass prairie.

name: Alagnak
summary: The headwaters of Alagnak Wild River lie within the rugged Aleutian Range of neighboring Katmai National Park and Preserve. Meandering west towards Bristol Bay and the Bering Sea, the Alagnak traverses the beautiful Alaska Peninsula, providing an unparalleled opportunity to experience the unique wilderness, wildlife, and cultural heritage of southwest Alaska.

image.caption: salmon in Alagnak River
image.altText: underwater photo of salmon swimming in river

name: Alcatraz Island
summary: Alcatraz reveals stories of American incarceration, justice, and our common humanity. This small island was once a fort, a military prison, and a maximum security federal penitentiary. In 1969, the Indians of All Tribes occupied Alcatraz for 19 months in the name of freedom and Native American civil rights. We invite you to explore Alcatraz's complex history and natural beauty.

image.caption: Alcatraz Island
image.altText: View of the Alcatraz Lighthouse and Island from the water

name: Aleutian Islands World War II
summary: The remote Aleutian Islands, home to the Unangax̂ (Aleut) people for over 8,000 years, became a fiercely contested Pacific battleground in World War II. Some Unangax̂ were taken from their homelands as Japanese prisoners of war while the others were evacuated from the islands by the government. Both groups suffered greatly during the war, and some would never return to their villages.

image.caption: A homeland changed
image.altText: Group of people around a Russian cross in tall grass

name: Alibates Flint Quarries
summary: 13,000 years ago, Alibates Flint was used by mammoth hunters as a source of flint for tools. Learn how important this site was to the survival, commerce, and culture of the people of the High Plains.

image.caption: Turtle Petroglyph
image.altText: Turtle Petroglyph at Antelope Creek Village Site

name: Allegheny Portage Railroad
summary: The first railroad to cross the Allegheny Mountains, the Allegheny Portage Railroad was the final piece of the Pennsylvania Main Line Canal. "The Portage" opened in 1834, marking the first time that there was one, direct route between Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. All things to all people, it served merchants, passengers, slaves in pursuit of freedom, and soldiers from the Mexican War.

image.caption: Engine House 6 Exhibit Shelter and the Lemon House
image.altText: Engine House and tavern

name: Amache
summary: Amache, also known as the Granada Relocation Center, near Granada, Colorado was one of ten incarceration sites established by the War Relocation Authority during World War II to unjustly incarcerate Japanese Americans. Over 10,000 people, most American citizens, were incarcerated at Amache from 1942 to 1945.

image.caption: Water tower
image.altText: A water tower on the horizon next to trees

name: Amistad
summary: An oasis in the desert, Amistad National Recreation Area consists of the US portion of the International Amistad Reservoir. Amistad, a Spanish word meaning "friendship," is known for excellent water-based recreation, camping, hiking, and rich cultural history dating back nearly 5,000 years. Amistad is also home to a wide variety of plant and animal life both above and below the water.

image.caption: Amistad Reservoir and Hwy 90 Bridge
image.altText: Sunset over Amistad Reservoir with Highway 90 bridge to left of photo going over the reservoir and i

name: American Memorial
summary: American Memorial Park honors the American and Marianas people who gave their lives during the Marianas Campaign of World War II. At the park, memorials stand in tribute to the courage and sacrifice of the US Servicemen and Chamorro and Carolinian civilians who were killed in the battles between the United States and Japan that took place on Saipan, Tinian, and the Philippine Sea in 1944.

image.caption: Lawn at American Memorial Park
image.altText: Large lawn in front of the memorial.

name: Anacostia
summary: Welcome to Anacostia Park, your neighborhood national park in the heart of Washington, DC! Enjoy exercise along the river trail or relax by the water, Anacostia Park is a breath of fresh air and a space to unwind amid a bustling city.

image.caption: Anacostia Drive
image.altText: Aerial view of Anacostia Drive and the playground

name: Andersonville
summary: Nearly 13,000 men died on these grounds, a site that became infamous even before the Civil War ended. Their burial grounds became Andersonville National Cemetery, where veterans continue to be buried today. This place, where tens of thousands suffered captivity so others could be free, is also home to the National Prisoner of War Museum and serves as a memorial to all American prisoners of war.

image.caption: Historic Site of Camp Sumter Civil War Military Prison at Andersonville
image.altText: A cannon sits out in front of a replica of part of the wooden stockade walls once at Andersonville

name: Aniakchak
summary: Given its remote location and challenging weather conditions, Aniakchak is one of the most wild and least visited places in the National Park System. This landscape is a vibrant reminder of Alaska's location in the volcanically active "Ring of Fire," as it is home to an impressive six mile (10 km) wide, 2,500 ft (762 m) deep caldera formed during a massive volcanic eruption 3,500 years ago.

image.caption: Floating the Gates of Aniakchak
image.altText: A lone raft floats the Aniakchak Wild River as it flows through the "Gates"

name: Andrew Johnson
summary: Andrew Johnson's complex presidency (1865-69) illustrates the Constitution at work following the Civil War. As the President and Congress disagreed on Reconstruction methods, the Constitution served as their guide on balance of powers, vetoes, and impeachment. In the end, it evolved as a living document with pivotal amendments on freedom, citizenship, and voting rights - topics still vital today.

image.caption: Andrew Johnson Homestead
image.altText: Andrew Johnson Homestead with snow

name: Antietam
summary: 23,000 soldiers were killed, wounded or missing after twelve hours of savage combat on September 17, 1862. The Battle of Antietam ended the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia's first invasion into the North and led Abraham Lincoln to issue the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation.

image.caption: Memorial Illumination
image.altText: luminaries placed by Maryland Monument with dramatic orange red clouds

name: Appomattox Court House
summary: On April 9, 1865, the surrender of the Army of Northern Virginia in the McLean House in the village of Appomattox Court House, Virginia signaled the effective end of the nation's largest war. Questions remained: could the nation reunite as one? How would emancipation be realized?

image.caption: McLean House
image.altText: A brick two story home with white pillars and railings.

name: Apostle Islands
summary: Apostle Islands National Lakeshore, located at the northern tip of Wisconsin's Bayfield Peninsula, features 21 stunning islands, a scenic 12-mile shoreline along Lake Superior, and is located within the ancestral homeland of the Ojibwe people. Established in 1970, the park showcases picturesque sea caves, sandy beaches, and the largest collection of lighthouses in the National Park system.

image.caption: Stockton Island
image.altText: Photograph of Lake Superior sandstone rock stack under a blue sky.

name: Arlington House, The Robert E. Lee Memorial
summary: Arlington House is the nation’s memorial to Robert E. Lee. It honors him for specific reasons, including his role in promoting peace and reunion after the Civil War. In a larger sense it exists as a place of study and contemplation of the meaning of some of the most difficult aspects of American history: military service; sacrifice; citizenship; duty; loyalty; slavery and freedom.

image.caption: Arlington House, The Robert E. Lee Memorial
image.altText: Columns of Arlington House

name: Arkansas Post
summary: Located at the confluence of two rivers, Arkansas Post has served as a gathering place for many cultures throughout human history - it represents cultural cooperation, conflict, synthesis, and diversity.

image.caption: Arkansas Post National Monument
image.altText: confluence of two rivers

name: Assateague Island
summary: Want to live on the edge? Visit a place recreated each day by ocean wind and waves. Life on Assateague Island has adapted to an existence on the move. Explore sandy beaches, salt marshes, maritime forests and coastal bays. Rest, relax, recreate and enjoy some time on the edge of the continent.

image.caption: Wild Horses on the dunes at Assateague
image.altText: Wild horses on the dunes at Assateague

name: Aztec Ruins
summary: Aztec Ruins has some of the best-preserved Chacoan structures of its kind. Learn more about the ancestral Pueblo people in the park's museum and explore the Aztec West great house to see exceptionally advanced architecture, original wooden beams, and a restored Great Kiva. Aztec Ruins is a deeply sacred place to many Indigenous peoples across the American Southwest. Please visit with respect.

image.caption: Great Kiva in Aztec West plaza
image.altText: Reconstructed stone kiva amidst stone ruins

name: Bandelier
summary: Bandelier National Monument protects over 33,000 acres of ruggedly beautiful canyon and mesa country. Petroglyphs, dwellings carved into the soft rock cliffs, and standing masonry walls pay tribute to the early days of a culture that still survives in the surrounding communities.

image.caption: Tyuonyi
image.altText: the village of Tyuonyi

name: Baltimore-Washington
summary: This 29-mile highway connects Baltimore, MD and Washington, D.C. The parkway has carried visitors to and from the capital city since 1954.

image.caption: Baltimore Washington Parkway
image.altText: Gladys Noon Spellman sign on the Baltimore Washington Parkway

name: Bering Land Bridge
summary: Bering Land Bridge National Preserve lies at the continental crossroad that greatly influenced the distribution of life in the Western Hemisphere during the Pleistocene Epoch. It is a vital landscape for Indigenous communities who depend on the land just as their ancestors did for many generations. It is a wild and ecologically healthy landscape unlike any other.

image.caption: Wet Muskox
image.altText: Three wet muskox stand in a line.

name: Bent's Old Fort
summary: In the 1840s the Arkansas River was the border between territory claimed by the United States and Mexico. Located along the river, Bent's Fort was an adobe trading post on the Santa Fe Trail, where traders, trappers, travelers, and the Cheyenne and Arapaho tribes came together in peaceful terms for trade. Today, a reconstructed fort allows visitors to explore the front line of Westward Expansion.

image.caption: Plaza visitors
image.altText: A group of visitors stand around a large wooden apparatus in a plaza courtyard.

name: Belmont-Paul Women's Equality
summary: Home to the National Woman's Party for more than 90 years, this was the epicenter of the struggle for women's rights. From this house in the shadow of the U.S. Capitol and Supreme Court, Alice Paul and the NWP developed innovative strategies and tactics to advocate for the Equal Rights Amendment and equality for women. President Barack Obama designated the national monument on April 12, 2016.

image.caption: Belmont-Paul Women's Equality NM House
image.altText: Belmont-Paul Women's Equality NM House

name: Bighorn Canyon
summary: The vast, wild landscape of Bighorn Canyon National Recreation Area offers visitors unparalleled opportunities to immerse themselves in the natural world, and experience the wonders of this extraordinary place. With over 120,000 acres, one can find an astounding diversity in ecosystems, wildlife, and more than 10,000 years of human history to explore.

name: Birmingham Civil Rights
summary: In 1963, images of snarling police dogs unleashed against non-violent protesters and of children being sprayed with high-pressure hoses appeared in print and television news around the world. These dramatic scenes of violent police aggression against civil rights protesters in Birmingham, Alabama were vivid examples of segregation and racial injustice in America.

image.caption: Mural Sculpture of the four little girls
image.altText: 4 separate statues of the four little girls who were killed in the 16th st Baptist Church bombing

name: Big Cypress
summary: The freshwaters of the Big Cypress Swamp, essential to the health of the neighboring Everglades, support the rich marine estuaries along Florida's southwest coast. Conserving over 729,000 acres of this vast swamp, Big Cypress National Preserve contains a mixture of tropical and temperate plant communities that are home to diverse wildlife, including the Endangered Florida panther.

image.caption: Small Alligator
image.altText: A small alligator basking on top of dry vegetation.

name: Big Hole
summary: On August 9, 1877, gunshots shattered a chilly dawn on a sleeping camp of nımí·pu· (Nez Perce). By the time the smoke cleared on August 10, almost 90 nımí·pu· were dead, along with 31 soldiers and volunteers. Big Hole National Battlefield was created to honor all who were there.

image.caption: Battlefield at Dawn
image.altText: Multiple tepee poles and a river are silhouetted against a dawn sky.

name: Big South Fork
summary: Encompassing 125,000 acres of the Cumberland Plateau, Big South Fork National River and Recreation Area protects the free-flowing Big South Fork of the Cumberland River and its tributaries. The area boasts miles of scenic gorges and sandstone bluffs, is rich with natural and historic features and has been developed to provide visitors with a wide range of outdoor recreational activities.

image.caption: Big South Fork NRRA in Fall
image.altText: Big South Fork NRRA in Fall

name: Big Thicket
summary: Life of all types abounds in the Big Thicket. This national preserve protects the incredible diversity of life found where multiple habitats meet in southeast Texas. Hiking trails and waterways meander through nine different ecosystems, from longleaf pine forests to cypress-lined bayous. It is a place of discovery, a place to wander and explore, a place to marvel at the richness of nature.

image.caption: Edgewater
image.altText: Reflections of twisting tupelo trees in calm water below a green canopy.

name: Blue Ridge
summary: A Blue Ridge Parkway experience is unlike any other: a slow-paced and relaxing drive revealing stunning long-range vistas and close-up views of the rugged mountains and pastoral landscapes of the Appalachian Highlands. The Parkway meanders for 469 miles, protecting a diversity of plants and animals, and providing opportunities for enjoying all that makes this region of the country so special.

image.caption: Mabry Mill
image.altText: Summer colors at Mabry Mill

name: Blackstone River Valley
summary: The Blackstone River powered America's entry into the Age of Industry. The success of Samuel Slater's cotton spinning mill in Pawtucket, RI touched off a chain reaction that changed how people worked and where they lived. Learn how this revolution transformed the landscape of the Blackstone Valley and the United States. The Visitor Center at Old Slater Mill is closed for the winter season.

image.caption: Slater Mill Site
image.altText: Slater Mill, Wilkinson Mill and Brown House at Blackstone River Valley NHP

name: Blackwell School
summary: Written by prejudice rather than law, the story of the Blackwell School is one of “separate but equal” education for Mexican and Mexican American citizens of Marfa, Texas. Built in 1909, the school serves as a significant example of how racism and cultural disparity dominated education and social systems in the United States during this period of de facto segregation from 1889-1965.

image.caption: Blackwell School East Exterior
image.altText: cream colored building with two windows and a wooden doorway with steps leading up to it.

name: Bluestone
summary: The Bluestone River and the rugged and ancient gorge it has carved is a richly diverse and scenic area of the southern Appalachians. Bluestone National Scenic River is preserved as a living landscape that provides an unspoiled experience for visitors and a haven for a variety of plants and animals. The park protects a 10.5-mile section of the Bluestone River in southern West Virginia.

image.caption: Bluestone River
image.altText: Bluestone River

name: Boston African American
summary: Centered on the north slope of Beacon Hill, the African American community of 1800s Boston led the city and the nation in the fight against slavery and injustice. These remarkable men and women, together with their allies, were leaders in the Abolition Movement, the Underground Railroad, the Civil War, and the early struggle for equal rights and education.

image.caption: The African Meeting House
image.altText: View from the pulpit at the African Meeting House, which has rows of benches and an upper gallery

name: Boston Harbor Islands
summary: . . . where you can walk a Civil War-era fort, view historic lighthouses, explore tide pools, hike lush trails, camp under the stars, or relax while fishing, picnicking, or swimming—all within reach of downtown Boston. Youth programs, visitor services, research, wildlife management, and more are coordinated on the park's 34 islands and peninsulas by the Boston Harbor Islands Partnership.

image.caption: Beach Dancing
image.altText: A child dancing on the beach at dusk

name: Boston
summary: Discover how one city could be the Cradle of Liberty, site of the first major battle of American Revolution, and home to many who espoused that freedom can be extended to all.

image.caption: Town Meetings at Faneuil Hall
image.altText: A desk with paper and two sets of quills frame a person in colonial wear standing in the aisle.

name: Booker T. Washington
summary: Booker T. Washington was born a slave in April 1856 on the 207-acre farm of James Burroughs. After the Civil War, Washington became the first principal of Tuskegee Normal and Industrial School. Later as an adviser, author and orator, his past would influence his philosophies as the most influential African American of his era. Come explore his birthplace.

image.caption: The reconstructed kitchen cabin and smoke house in the snow
image.altText: Back side of kitchen cabin and smokehouse in snow with blue sky and trees

name: Brices Cross Roads
summary: The Confederate victory at Brices Cross Roads was a significant victory for Major General Nathan Bedford Forrest, but its long-term effect on the war proved costly for the Confederates.

image.caption: Brices Cross Roads National Battlefield Site
image.altText: Two large trees and a flagpole flying an American flag overlooking a stone monument and cannons

name: Brown v. Board of Education
summary: The path to equality has been anything but smooth. It's taken courage and dedication by everyday people coming together for a common goal to carry the country toward true equality. Parents, teachers, secretaries, welders, ministers, and students drove their communities, and the country along with them, toward justice in a series of often unsteady turns leading to the Brown v. Board decision.

image.caption: Brown v Board NHP Exterior
image.altText: Brown v Board National Historical Park

name: Buffalo
summary: Established in 1972, Buffalo National River flows freely for 135 miles and is one of the few remaining undammed rivers in the lower 48 states. Once you arrive, prepare to journey from running rapids to quiet pools while surrounded by massive bluffs as you cruise through the Ozark Mountains down to the White River.

image.caption: Indian Rockhouse
image.altText: A large bluff shelter near Buffalo Point.

name: Buck Island Reef
summary: Welcome to Buck Island Reef National Monument, called “the finest marine garden in the Caribbean Sea” by President John F. Kennedy. Snorkel the famous underwater trail, explore endangered elkhorn coral reefs. Hike the trails on the 176-acre island to the observation platform for an unparallel view. Discover a vibrant world above and beneath the waves in this Caribbean paradise.

image.caption: Elkhorn Coral at Buck Island Reef NM
image.altText: Snorkeler swimming by Elkhorn Coral at Buck Island Reef NM.

name: Cabrillo
summary: In 1542, Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo climbed out of his boat and onto shore, becoming the first European to set foot on what is now the West Coast of the United States. Cabrillo National Monument not only tells the story of this 16th-century exploration but also houses a wealth of cultural and natural resources. Join us and embark on your own Voyage of Exploration.

image.caption: Rocky Intertidal Zone
image.altText: Tidepools at Cabrillo

name: Canyon de Chelly
summary: This canyon is home to Diné families who raise livestock, grow crops and live here. People have lived in these canyons for nearly 5,000 years, which is longer than anyone has lived continuously on the Colorado Plateau. In this place called Tsegi, their homes and images tell us their stories. Today, the park and Navajo Nation work together to manage the rich cultural and natural resources.

image.caption: Canyon Hike
image.altText: Hiking in the canyon

name: Castle Clinton
summary: Located at the southern tip of Manhattan, Castle Clinton marks the place where New York City began and reflects the growth of both the city and the nation. Built to defend the harbor during the War of 1812, it has since welcomed theatergoers, immigrants, and sightseers—and today continues to greet millions of visitors to New York Harbor.

image.caption: Castle Clinton National Monument
image.altText: Castle Clinton NM Entrance

name: Cape Cod
summary: The great Outer Beach described by Thoreau in the 1800s is protected within the national seashore. Forty miles of pristine sandy beach, marshes, ponds, and uplands support diverse species. Lighthouses, cultural landscapes, and wild cranberry bogs offer a glimpse of Cape Cod's past and continuing ways of life. Swimming beaches and walking and biking trails beckon today's visitors.

image.caption: Sunrise Waves
image.altText: A curling wave breaks against the backdrop of a pink sunrise.

name: Casa Grande Ruins
summary: An Ancestral Sonoran Desert People's farming community and "Great House" are preserved at Casa Grande Ruins. Whether a gathering place for people or simply a waypoint marker in an extensive system of canals and trading partners, the structures are a large part of the story of this site. Explore the history and stories of an extended network of communities and irrigation canals.

image.caption: Great House
image.altText: eathern building under modern roof structure

name: Cape Hatteras
summary: The sound of ocean waves, the starry night sky, or the calm of the salt marshes, you can experience it all. Shaped by the forces of water, wind, and storms these islands are ever changing. The plants, wildlife, and people who live here adapt continually. Whether you are enjoying the beach, kayaking the sound, or climbing the Cape Hatteras Lighthouse there is something for everyone to explore!

image.caption: Cape Hatteras Lighthouse
image.altText: A beach landscape with the black and white spiraled lighthouse in the background

name: Cape Krusenstern
summary: A bridge to the past and a land for the future, Cape Krusenstern National Monument protects approximately 560,000 acres of diverse Arctic coastal, and upland ecosystems. Inhabited by the Iñupiaq people since time-immemorial, over 5,000 years of sequential human use is documented in the 114 successive beach ridges. Rich connections to the land and waters are preserved through subsistence practices.

image.caption: Muskox and Geese
image.altText: muskox standing on the tundra

name: Cape Lookout
summary: A boat ride three miles off-shore brings you to the barrier islands of Cape Lookout National Seashore. Horse watching, shelling, fishing, birding, camping, lighthouse climbing, and touring historic villages--there’s something for everyone at Cape Lookout. Be sure to bring all the food, water, and supplies you need (and carry your trash out of the park) when visiting these remote beaches.

image.caption: Cape Lookout Lighthouse
image.altText: : Black & white patterned tower of the Cape Lookout Lighthouse stands against a blue & white cloud f

name: Cape Henry Memorial
designation: Part of Colonial National Historical Park
summary: English colonists first landed here in April 1607, erected a wooden cross and gave thanks for a successful crossing to a new land. In 1781, Americans could watch from these same sand dunes the largest naval battle of the Revolutionary War. Our French Allies defeated a British fleet just off this shore to set the stage for General George Washington's victory at Yorktown.

image.caption: Memorial Cross
image.altText: Gray stone cross monument in front of a low stone wall at the end of a flagstone path

name: Castle Mountains
summary: Castle Mountains represents some of the most unique elements of the Mojave Desert. Nestled between the Nevada state line and Mojave National Preserve, the nearly 21,000 acres of Castle Mountains boasts Joshua tree forests, unbroken natural landscapes, rare desert grasslands, and rich human history. This intriguing area provides serenity and solitude from nearby metropolitan areas.

image.caption: Red Rocks Outcropping
image.altText: Red rocks frame a stand of Joshua trees and sage brush.

name: Canaveral
summary: Discover a dynamic barrier island shaped by dunes, coastal hammocks, and Mosquito Lagoon. Walk among ancient Timucua shell mounds and connect with thousands of years of human history. Immerse yourself in a protected sanctuary where diverse plants and wildlife thrive—making Canaveral National Seashore a place where nature, history, and discovery come together.

image.caption: Apollo Beach
image.altText: Dune plants, beach, and ocean.

name: Camp Nelson
summary: The US Army established Camp Nelson as a fortified supply depot in April 1863. Over the next 3 years, the site evolved into a massive recruitment and training center for United States Colored Troops and a refugee camp for their families. It served as a shelter for civilians fleeing war and for enslaved people hoping to secure their freedom and aid in the destruction of slavery.

image.caption: Camp Nelson National Monument Visitor Center
image.altText: A paved path leads to a gray wooden building with US Flag flying.

name: Cane River Creole
summary: The Cane River region is home to a unique culture; the Creoles. Generations of the same families of workers, enslaved and tenant, and owners lived on these lands for over 200 years. The park tells their stories and preserves the cultural landscape of Oakland and Magnolia Plantations, two of the most intact Creole cotton plantations in the United States.

image.caption: Oakland Plantation Quarters
image.altText: A small cabin sits beneath the branches of a Live Oak in the Oakland Plantation Quarters.

name: Carl Sandburg Home
summary: Current Status: Pedestrian detour in place from main parking lot. Grounds / trails open dawn till dusk 7 days a week. Barn open 7 days a week 10-4. Bookstore / Visitor Center open Tuesday - Sunday 9-5. Interagency passes can be purchased at Visitor Center.

image.caption: Carl Sandburg's Study
image.altText: A view of Sandburg's study as visitors see it today

name: Castillo de San Marcos
summary: Built by the Spanish in St. Augustine to defend Florida and the Atlantic trade route, Castillo de San Marcos National Monument preserves the oldest masonry fortification in the continental United States and interprets more than 450 years of cultural intersections.

image.caption: Castillo Drawbridge
image.altText: Drawbridge entrance to the Castillo de San Marcos

name: Catoctin Mountain
summary: President Franklin D. Roosevelt created programs to give people a chance to rebuild their lives from the Great Depression. The Works Progress Administration and the Civilian Conservation Corps gave this land a second opportunity and through re-growth, a new role as a recreation area.

image.caption: Chimney Rock Vista
image.altText: Rock formation with mountains in the background

name: Capulin Volcano
summary: Part of the 8,000 square mile Raton-Clayton Volcanic Field, Capulin Volcano showcases the volcanic geology of northeastern New Mexico. The views are spectacular day or night, with views of 4 different states from the volcanic rim and one of the darkest night skies in the country. Whether it's a quick stop or a day's trip, enjoy exploring the landscape of this unique volcano!

image.caption: Capulin Volcano
image.altText: A cloud shrouded volcano rises behind a field of yellow flowers.

name: Carter G. Woodson Home
summary: Before Dr. Carter G. Woodson, there was very little accurate written history about the lives and experiences of Americans of African descent. Today a National Historic Site, Dr. Woodson’s home served as the headquarters for the Association for the Study of African American Life and History. Dr. Woodson established Negro History Week here in 1926, which we celebrate today as Black History Month.

image.caption: Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site
image.altText: The restored facades of three historic Victorian row-homes on an urban street in Washington, DC

name: Cedar Creek & Belle Grove
summary: Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley has a long and rich heritage that still inspires today. Native Americans first shaped the land, followed by colonists and settlers. The fertile valley became an important wheat-growing region in the 1800s. It also witnessed dramatic Civil War campaigns, including the Battle of Cedar Creek, a decisive Federal victory that helped bring the war to an end.

image.caption: Belle Grove Manor House
image.altText: American flag bunting hangs from the porch on a limestone building with a white portico.

name: Cedar Breaks
summary: Crowning the Grand Staircase, Cedar Breaks sits at over 10,000 feet and looks down into a half-mile deep geologic amphitheater. Come wander among timeless bristlecone pines, stand in lush meadows of wildflowers, ponder crystal-clear night skies and experience the richness of our subalpine forest.

image.caption: Cedar Breaks Information Center
image.altText: A small log cabin with a stone chimney on one side.

name: César E. Chávez
summary: Yes, we can! Widely recognized as the most important Latino leader in the United States during the twentieth century, Cesar Chavez led farm workers and supporters in the establishment of the country's first permanent agricultural union. His leadership brought sustained international attention to the plight of U.S. farm workers, and secured for them higher wages and safer working conditions.

image.caption: Courtyard at Visitor Center Entrance
image.altText: A walkway with a fountain

name: Chamizal
summary: Chamizal is more than just an urban park to recreate or enjoy a quiet afternoon. These grounds are a reminder of the harmonious settlement of a 100-year boundary dispute between the United States and Mexico. We celebrate the cultures of the borderlands to promote the same mutual respect that helped to diplomatically resolve an international disagreement.

image.caption: Mountain View
image.altText: a bench next to a tree with U.S. and Mexican flags flying against a mountain background

name: Chattahoochee River
summary: Today the river valley attracts us for so many reasons. Take a solitary walk to enjoy nature’s display, raft leisurely through the rocky shoals with friends, fish the misty waters as the sun comes up, or have a picnic on a Sunday afternoon. Get Outdoors and experience your Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area as you have never done before.

image.caption: Family Time
image.altText: Two adult Great Blue Herons stand watch over their 3 young chicks in the nest.

name: Chickamauga & Chattanooga
summary: In 1863, Union and Confederate forces fought for control of Chattanooga - a gateway to the Confederacy. The Confederates were victorious at nearby Chickamauga in September. However, renewed fighting in Chattanooga that November provided Union troops victory and control of the city. After the fighting, a Confederate soldier ominously wrote, "This...is the death-knell of the Confederacy."

image.caption: Kelley Cabin on Chickamauga Battlefield
image.altText: Kelley Cabin

name: Chaco Culture
summary: Explore the monumental structures and breathtaking landscape at Chaco, a thriving regional center for the ancestral Pueblo people from 850 to 1250 CE (Common Era), through hiking & biking trails, ranger guided tours & programs, and more. Chaco Canyon is a sacred and deeply personal place for many Indigenous peoples throughout the Southwest. Please visit with respect.

image.caption: Sandstone Walls
image.altText: Colorful sandstone walls with two open sections in the middle that look like doorways.

name: Chickasaw
summary: Springs, streams, lakes - whatever its form, water is the attraction at Chickasaw National Recreation Area.

image.caption: Lincoln Bridge
image.altText: Lincoln Bridge with Travertine Creek flowing below

name: Chiricahua
summary: Explore rhyolite pinnacles and balanced rocks on foot or by car. Relax at the campground under star-filled, dark skies. See how a mountain range rising between two deserts creates a home for diverse wildlife. Imagine history here. Prehistoric peoples, Apaches, Buffalo Soldiers, Civilian Conservation Corps, ranchers, and homesteaders inhabited Chiricahua.

image.caption: View from Massai Point
image.altText: Many rock pinnacles with a valley and mountain range in background

name: Chesapeake & Ohio Canal
summary: Preserving America's early transportation history, the C&O Canal began as a dream of passage to Western wealth. Operating for nearly 100 years the canal was a lifeline for communities along the Potomac River as coal, lumber, and agricultural products floated down the waterway to market. Today it endures as a pathway for discovering historical, natural, and recreational treasures.

image.caption: Towpath along Lush Canal
image.altText: A gravel travel next to a watered canal surrounded by bright greenery

name: Charles Pinckney
summary: Charles Pinckney was a principal author and signer of the United States Constitution and went on to be a political leader in South Carolina for over 40 years. The park preserves Snee Farm, one of his plantation properties, where visitors can learn about the politician's influences on Charleston, the African people he enslaved, plantation operations, and the legacy of Pinckney's life.

image.caption: Historic House and Grounds
image.altText: 1828 Lowcountry cottage and grounds

name: Christiansted
summary: Christiansted National Historic Site was established in 1952 as the first unit of the National Park Service in the Virgin Islands of the United States. Covering over seven acres the park tells the stories about Danish economy and ways of life, and the interactions of people in Europe, Africa, West Indies, and North America during the Danish era of occupation of the Virgin Islands (1734-1917).

image.caption: Fort Christiansvaern
image.altText: View of the Christiansted NHS complex

name: Little Rock Central High School
summary: In 1957, Little Rock Central High School was the epicenter of confrontation and a catalyst for change as the fundamental test for the United States to enforce African American civil rights following Brown v. Board of Education. Learn how the sacrifice and struggle endured by the Little Rock Nine have provided opportunities and opened doors for those seeking education around the world.

image.caption: Little Rock Central High School
image.altText: The front facade of Little Rock Central High School

name: Charles Young Buffalo Soldiers
summary: Throughout his life, Charles Young overcame countless obstacles in his ascent to prominence. In spite of overt racism and stifling inequality, Young rose through the military ranks to become one of the most respected leaders of his time. A well-rounded man with a steadfast devotion to duty, Young led by example and inspired a generation of new leaders.

image.caption: Youngsholm, September 2025
image.altText: A large grey house with dark grey shutters with a green lawn out front under a blue sky

name: Carlisle Federal Indian Boarding School
summary: More than 7,800 children from 140 Tribes went to the Carlisle School from 1879 to 1918. The National Park Service will collaborate with families, affiliated Tribal Nations, the US Army, historians, and partners to develop resources and share the story of the children, families, and communities impacted by Carlisle Federal Indian Boarding School.

name: City Of Rocks
summary: Described by California Trail emigrants as “a city of tall spires,” “steeple rocks,” and “the silent city,” this awe-inspiring landscape continues to captivate. Today, it beckons rock climbers, hikers, campers, hunters, and adventurers with its dramatic scenery, fascinating geology, and echoes of the Old West. The Silent City is ready for you to explore.

image.caption: City of Rocks Granite
image.altText: Snow dusted granite formations jut up from a mountainous juniper covered landscape.

name: Clara Barton
summary: Clara Barton dedicated her life and energies to help others in times of need - both home and abroad, in peacetime as well as during military emergencies. Glen Echo was her home the last 15 years of her life, and the structure illustrates her dedication and concern for those less fortunate than herself.

image.caption: Clara Barton National Historic Site Front View
image.altText: two and half story wooden frame house with double porch and stone corner posts.

name: Constitution Gardens
summary: Officially established in 1965, National Mall and Memorial Parks actually protects some of the older parkland in the National Park System. Areas within this premier park provide visitors with ample opportunities to commemorate presidential legacies; honor the courage and sacrifice of war veterans; and celebrate the United States commitment to freedom and equality.

image.caption: Constitution Garden
image.altText: Shot of the Garden Pond with the Washington Monument in the background

name: Colorado
summary: Colorado National Monument preserves one of the grand landscapes of the American West. But this treasure is much more than a monument. Towering monoliths exist within a vast plateau and canyon panorama. You can experience sheer-walled, red rock canyons along the twists and turns of Rim Rock Drive, where you may spy bighorn sheep and soaring eagles.

image.caption: Independence Monument View
image.altText: sandstone spire hundreds of feet tall stands above sparsely vegetated canyon bottom and cliffs

name: Colonial
summary: On May 13, 1607, Jamestown was established as the first permanent English settlement in North America. Three cultures came together – European, Virginia Indian and African–to create a new society that would eventually seek independence from Great Britain. On October 19, 1781, American and French troops defeated the British at Yorktown in the last major battle of the American Revolutionary War.

image.caption: Surrender Field
image.altText: Wooden split rail fencing and flowering trees surround a grassy field behind an interpretive panel

name: Coltsville
summary: When Samuel Colt started his Hartford factory on the banks of the Connecticut River in 1847, it followed years of mismanagement and failure. Soon, demand for Colt's revolver would change his fortunes and the Colt empire was born. Following Colt's untimely death in 1862, his wife, Elizabeth Colt, would lead the company to its legendary status, and influence Hartford for over 40 years.

image.caption: Colt Armory Complex
image.altText: Blue dome atop a large factory behind a river

name: Coronado
summary: It was a journey of conquest filled with exploration, wonder - and cruelty. Inspired by tales of vast cities of gold, 339 European soldiers and over a thousand Aztec allies embarked on an epic journey through arid deserts and rugged mountains. They encountered rich traditions and brought new technologies. The resulting collision and combination of cultures reverberates today.

image.caption: Wildflowers and Montezuma Peak
image.altText: Agave stalks and wildflowers with mountains in the distance

name: Cowpens
summary: A pasturing area at the time of the battle, this Revolutionary War site commemorates the place where Daniel Morgan and his army turned the flanks of Banastre Tarleton's British army. This classic military tactic, known as a double envelopment, secured a patriot victory.

image.caption: Sunrise on Green River Road
image.altText: The sun is coming up on the battlefield in the direction that the Americans would have been facing.

name: Craters Of The Moon
summary: Craters of the Moon is a vast ocean of lava flows with scattered islands of cinder cones and sagebrush. We invite you to explore this "weird and scenic landscape" where yesterday's volcanic events are likely to continue tomorrow.

image.caption: A Sea of Lava
image.altText: A close-up shot of a folded, waving sea of lava rock, with mountains in the far distance.

name: Cumberland Gap
summary: Cumberland Gap was the first great gateway to the west. Come follow the path of bison, Native Americans, longhunters, and pioneers. Walk where 300,000 people crossed the Appalachians to settle America. Explore 85 miles of trails and 14,000 acres of wilderness. Stand in 3 states at once. Explore a cave, see Hensley Settlement, or camp under the stars. Come find your connection to Cumberland Gap.

image.caption: Hensley Settlement
image.altText: Hensley Settlement

name: Cumberland Island
summary: St Marys is the gateway to Cumberland Island, Georgia's largest and southernmost barrier island. Here pristine maritime forests, undeveloped beaches and wide marshes whisper the stories of both man and nature. Natives, missionaries, enslaved African Americans and Wealthy Industrialists all walked here. Cumberland Island is also home to over 9,800 acres of Congressionally designated Wilderness.

image.caption: Vegetated Dunes
image.altText: Sand dunes covered with shrubs and grasses

name: Curecanti
summary: Three reservoirs and surrounding lands make up this recreation area in western Colorado. It is a landscape of tradeoffs; natural and human made features exist together. Geologic wonders are abundant from the sagebrush shrublands to forests. Visitors can experience the park year-round on both land and water.

image.caption: Blue Mesa Reservoir
image.altText: A single boat floating out in a reservoir. Mesas surrounding the area are reflected on the water.

name: Civil War Defenses of Washington
summary: On forested hills surrounding the nation's capital are the remnants of a complex system of Civil War fortifications. These strategic buttresses transformed the young capital into one of the world's most fortified cities. By 1865, 68 forts and 93 batteries armed with over 800 cannons encircled Washington, DC. Today, you can visit 18 of the original sites now managed by the National Park Service.

image.caption: Where Abraham Lincoln Stood
image.altText: A woman in a 19th-century dress stands along an earthwork fortification

name: Dayton Aviation Heritage
summary: Dayton Aviation Heritage National Historical Park was established to honor the lives and achievements of poet and author Paul Laurence Dunbar and aviation pioneers Wilbur and Orville Wright. Through perseverance and dedication Orville, Wilbur and Paul were able to overcome obstacles in their lives and leave their respective marks on history. Start your visit at one of our locations today.

image.caption: Wright-Dunbar Interpretive Center
image.altText: A three-story brick building with tall green windows and a tall photo mural on the glass wall

name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
summary: The Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial tells the story of one of America's greatest leaders of the 20th century.

image.caption: Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial Entrance
image.altText: Dwight D. Eisenhower Memorial Entrance

name: Devils Postpile
summary: Established in 1911 by presidential proclamation, Devils Postpile National Monument protects and preserves the Devils Postpile formation, the 101-foot high Rainbow Falls, and pristine mountain scenery. The formation is a rare sight in the geologic world and ranks as one of the world's finest examples of columnar basalt. Its' columns tower up to 60 feet and display a striking symmetry.

image.caption: Devils Postpile Formation
image.altText: The Devils Postpile basalt formation resembles tall columns.

name: De Soto
summary: In May 1539, Conquistador Hernando de Soto’s army of soldiers, hired mercenaries, craftsmen, and clergy made landfall in Tampa Bay. They were met with fierce resistance of indigenous people protecting their homelands. De Soto’s quest for glory and gold would be a four year, four thousand mile odyssey of intrigue, warfare, disease, and discovery that would form the history of the United States.

name: Devils Tower
summary: The Tower is an astounding geologic feature that protrudes out of the prairie surrounding the Black Hills. It is considered sacred by Northern Plains Indians and indigenous people. Hundreds of parallel cracks make it one of the finest crack climbing areas in North America. Devils Tower entices us to learn more, explore more and define our place in the natural and cultural world.

image.caption: Devils Tower looming above the trees
image.altText: Devils Tower looming above the trees

name: Delaware Water Gap
summary: Situated within the most densely populated region of the United States, Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area provides a unique opportunity to experience tranquil landscapes, rich human history, and striking scenery along 40 miles of the longest free-flowing river east of the Mississippi. The park offers year-round recreation including hiking, paddling, fishing, and hunting.

image.caption: Fulmer Falls
image.altText: A waterfall flows toward the viewer along a rocky riverbed.

name: Dinosaur
summary: 150 million years ago, dinosaurs roamed here. Their fossils are still embedded in the rocks. Today, mountains, desert, and rivers flowing in canyons support a variety of life. Petroglyphs reveal the lives and connections of Indigenous people to this land. Homesteaders and outlaws found refuge here. Whether your passion is science, adventure, history, or scenery, Dinosaur offers much to explore.

image.caption: Camarasaurus Skull
image.altText: the fossilized skull of camarasaurus dinosaur

name: Ebey's Landing
summary: This stunning landscape on the Salish Sea, with its rich farmland and promising seaport, lured the earliest American pioneers north of the Columbia River to Ebey’s Landing. Today Ebey’s Landing National Historical Reserve preserves the historical, agricultural and cultural traditions of both Native and Euro-American – while offering spectacular opportunities for recreation.

image.caption: View from the Bluff Overlook
image.altText: View from the Bluff Overlook

name: Edgar Allan Poe
summary: Described as horrifying, mystifying, and brilliant, Poe’s writing has engaged readers all over the world. The six years Edgar Allan Poe lived in Philadelphia were his happiest and most productive. Yet Poe also struggled with bad luck, personal demons and his wife’s illness. In Poe’s humble home, reflect on the human spirit surmounting crushing obstacles, and celebrate Poe’s astonishing creativity.

image.caption: Raven statue
image.altText: Color photo showing a large raven statue with wings outspread on a metal plinth.

name: Thomas Edison
summary: Today, the brick buildings on Main Street in West Orange, NJ seem quiet, betraying little evidence of the research, development, and innovation of their heyday. Visitors can step back in time to Thomas Edison’s home and laboratory, when machines were run by belts and pulleys and music was played on phonographs. Discover where America’s greatest inventor changed our world forever.

image.caption: Glenmont - Home of Thomas Edison
image.altText: Large salmon colored Victorian mansion with green lawn and blue sky

name: Effigy Mounds
summary: The mounds preserved here are considered sacred by many Americans, especially the Monument's 20 culturally associated American Indian tribes. A visit offers opportunities to contemplate the meanings of the mounds and the people who built them. The 200 plus American Indian mounds are located in one of the most picturesque sections of the Upper Mississippi River Valley.

image.caption: Marching Bear in Spring
image.altText: Bear Effigy Mounds with visitor walking nearby.

name: Eisenhower
summary: Eisenhower National Historic Site preserves the farm of General and 34th President Dwight D. Eisenhower. Adjacent to the Gettysburg battlefield, the farm served the president and first lady as a weekend retreat and as a meeting place for world leaders. With its peaceful setting and view of South Mountain, it was a respite from Washington, DC, and a backdrop for efforts to reduce Cold War tensions.

image.caption: Eisenhower home
image.altText: The Eisenhower home with Ike's putting green in the foreground

name: Ellis Island
designation: Part of Statue of Liberty National Monument
summary: Millions of Americans and people around the world have ancestors who came through Ellis Island. The Main Immigration Building was the epicenter of one of the greatest migrations in modern history. Today, Ellis Island is a memorial to all who pursued the American dream and have made this nation their adopted home.

image.caption: Ellis Island Museum of Immigration
image.altText: Beaux-Arts brick and limestone building with large arched windows and cupola-topped towers.

name: El Malpais
summary: The richly diverse volcanic landscape of El Malpais (el-mal-pie-EES) offers solitude, recreation, and adventure. Explore incredible geologic features such as young lava flows, cinder cones, lava tubes, and sandstone bluffs. While some may see a desolate environment, people have been adapting to and living in this extraordinary terrain for generations. Come visit the land of frozen fire!

image.caption: Sandstone Bluffs Overlook
image.altText: Yellow sandstone cliff at sunset with dark lava field in background

name: El Morro
summary: Imagine the refreshment of finding water after days of dusty travel. A reliable waterhole hidden at the base of a sandstone bluff made El Morro (the headland) a popular campsite for hundreds of years. Here, ancestral Puebloans, Spanish, and American travelers carved over 2,000 signatures, dates, messages, and petroglyphs. Make El Morro National Monument a stopping point on your travels.

image.caption: El Morro with Sunflowers
image.altText: El Morro with Sunflowers

name: Eleanor Roosevelt
summary: Visit the home of Eleanor Roosevelt. Here, Franklin and Eleanor entertained friends, the press, activists, and official state visitors in the relaxed atmosphere of Val-Kill. Explore the Roosevelt saga in the homes of Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt, the exhibits at the nation’s first Presidential Library, and over a thousand acres of gardens and trails.

image.caption: Val-Kill Cottage
image.altText: Val-Kill Cottage in the Summer

name: Eugene O'Neill
summary: America's only Nobel Prize-winning playwright, Eugene O'Neill, chose Northern California as his sanctuary at the pinnacle of his writing career. Secluded from the outside world within the serene walls of his Tao House, O'Neill crafted his final and most memorable masterpieces: The Iceman Cometh, Long Day's Journey Into Night, and A Moon for the Misbegotten.

image.caption: Eugene O'Neill Home in Danville, California
