U.S. forces cut off supplies to both Petersburg and the Confederate capital, Richmond. Today, the park preserves the sites of this pivotal campaign.

image.caption: Eastern Front Visitor Center
image.altText: Pictured is the front of the brick visitor center under a cloudless blue sky.

name: Petroglyph
summary: Petroglyph National Monument protects one of the largest petroglyph sites in North America, featuring designs and symbols carved onto volcanic rocks by Native Americans and Spanish settlers 400 to 700 years ago. These images are a valuable record of cultural expression and hold profound spiritual significance for contemporary Native Americans and for the descendants of the early Spanish settlers.

image.caption: Handprint petroglyphs in Piedras Marcadas Canyon
image.altText: Petroglyphs on dark boulders with a cloudy sky.

name: Perry's Victory & International Peace
summary: Perry's Victory and International Peace Memorial was established to honor those who fought in the Battle of Lake Erie, during the War of 1812, and to celebrate the long-lasting peace among Great Britain, Canada and the U.S. The Memorial, a Doric column, rising 352 feet over Lake Erie is situated 5 miles from the longest undefended border in the world.

image.caption: International flags at Memorial
image.altText: 9-3'x5' international flags line sidewalk that leads to a white building with green roof. Tall stone

name: New Jersey Pinelands
summary: This is truly a special place. It's classified as a United States Biosphere Reserve and in 1978 was established by Congress as the country’s first National Reserve. It includes portions of seven southern New Jersey counties, and encompasses over one-million acres of farms, forests and wetlands. It contains 56 communities, from hamlets to suburbs, with over 700,000 permanent residents.

name: Pipestone
summary: For over 3,000 years, Indigenous people have quarried the red stone at this site to make pipes used in prayer and ceremony - a tradition that continues to this day and makes this site sacred to many people.

image.caption: Tallgrass Prairie
image.altText: Purple and yellow wildflowers in a field of tall grass

name: Pictured Rocks
summary: Sandstone cliffs, beaches, waterfalls, sand dunes, inland lakes, deep forest, and wild shoreline beckon you to visit Pictured Rocks National Lakeshore. The power of Lake Superior shapes the park's coastal features and affects every ecosystem, creating a unique landscape to explore. Hiking, camping, sightseeing, and four-season outdoor opportunities abound.

image.caption: Autumn Colors at Miners Beach
image.altText: Golden and orange trees line a sandstone cliff rising above a beach on a cloudy autumn day

name: Piscataway
summary: Piscataway Park is home to bald eagles, beavers, deer, foxes, ospreys, and many other species. To complement the surroundings, the park has, in addition to a public fishing pier and two boardwalks over fresh water tidal wetlands, a variety of nature trails, meadows, and woodland areas. The Park is also home to National Colonial Farm.

image.caption: National Colonial Farm
image.altText: Building at National Colonial Farm at Piscataway Park

name: Pipe Spring
summary: The rich history of Pipe Spring and its flowing water comes alive as you explore the traditions of the Kaibab Paiute and the Mormon settlers through the museum, historic fort, cabins, and garden. Hike the Ridge Trail to enjoy geologic wonders, plants, and wildlife. Attend living history demonstrations and talks and be sure to visit with our amazing ranch animals!

image.caption: Milky Way over the Chuckwagon
image.altText: A glittering sky of stars glows above a historic covered wagon.

name: Port Chicago Naval Magazine
summary: On July 17, 1944, a massive explosion jolted the San Francisco East Bay area, shattering windows and lighting up the night sky. At Port Chicago Naval Magazine, 320 men were killed instantly when two ships loading ammunition for Pacific troops exploded, resulting in the worst home front disaster of WWII. The aftermath illuminated the issues of segregation and racial inequality in the military.

image.caption: Port Chicago Naval Magazine National Memorial
image.altText: Port Chicago Memorial

name: Poverty Point
summary: Now a nearly forgotten culture, Poverty Point at its peak 3,000 years ago was part of an enormous trading network that stretched for hundreds of miles across the continent. It was - and is - also an engineering marvel, the product of five million hours of labor. Explore the culture of a highly sophisticated people who left behind one of North America’s most important archeological sites.

name: Point Reyes
summary: From its thunderous ocean breakers crashing against rocky headlands and expansive sand beaches to its open grasslands, brushy hillsides, and forested ridges, Point Reyes offers visitors over 1500 species of plants and animals to discover. Home to several cultures over thousands of years, the Seashore preserves a tapestry of stories and interactions of people. Point Reyes awaits your exploration.

image.caption: Point Reyes Lighthouse
image.altText: A long concrete staircase down to a red roofed, white lighthouse on cliffs above the ocean.

name: Presidio of San Francisco
summary: For 218 years, the Presidio served as an army post for three nations. World and local events, from military campaigns to World Fairs and earthquakes, left their mark. Come enjoy the history and the natural beauty of the Presidio. Explore centuries of architecture. Reflect in a national cemetery. Walk along an historic airfield, through forests or to beaches, and admire spectacular vistas.

image.caption: San Francisco National Cemetery
image.altText: Rows of grave markers in the green grass of the cemetery as light shafts through misty trees.

name: Prince William Forest
summary: Prince William Forest Park is an oasis, a respite of quiet and calm. In 1936, Chopawamsic Recreation Area opened its gates to house children's 'relief' camps during the Great Depression. Renamed Prince William Forest Park in 1948, these fragrant woods and trickling streams have welcomed generations of campers, hikers, bikers and nature lovers. Discover Northern Virginia's best kept secret!

image.caption: Historic Park Sign for Chopawamsic RDA
image.altText: An original 1930's sign for Chopawamsic National Recreational Demonstration Area

name: Puʻukoholā Heiau
summary: How many places in America can you walk in the footsteps of a king? Where else has a stranded sailor risen up to become a great chief over an entire island? Where else can you experience the culminating event of a people, foretold from centuries past? Where else can you stand on a beach and watch as sharks pass over a submerged temple? Experience all this and much more – only at Pu'ukoholā Heiau!

image.caption: Puʻukoholā Heiau National Historic Site
image.altText: Heiau standing high above Pelekane Bay, as seen at sunset.

name: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau
summary: Imagine you had just broken the sacred laws, the kapu, and the only punishment was death. Your only chance of survival is to elude your pursuers and reach the Puʻuhonua, a place of refuge. The Puʻuhonua protected the kapu breaker, defeated warriors, as well as civilians during the time of battle. No physical harm could come to those who reached the boundaries of the Puʻuhonua.

image.caption: Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau National Historical Park
image.altText: Carved wooden kiʻi

name: Pullman
summary: In a growing Chicago neighborhood, diverse people and stories intertwined. All were seeking opportunity. Some succeeded. Others were limited—by race, gender, or economic status. Their stories came together in Pullman, a planned industrial community famed for its urban design and architecture.

image.caption: Welcome to Pullman National Historical Park
image.altText: The Pullman National Historical Park Visitor Center

name: Rainbow Bridge
summary: Rainbow Bridge is one of the world's largest known natural bridges. The span has undoubtedly inspired people throughout time--from the neighboring Native American tribes who consider Rainbow Bridge sacred, to the thousands of visitors from around the world who visit it each year. Please visit Rainbow Bridge in a spirit that honors and respects the cultures to whom it is sacred.

image.caption: Visitors Take in the Sight of Rainbow Bridge
image.altText: A large natural rock arch spans a canyon with people looking up at it.

name: Reconstruction Era
summary: The Reconstruction era,1861-1900 the historic period in which the United States grappled with the question of how to integrate millions of newly freed African Americans into social, political, economic, and labor systems, was a time of significant transformation. The people, places, and events in Beaufort County, South Carolina, reflect on the most important issues of this tumultuous time period.

image.caption: Brick Baptist Church
image.altText: A two story brick building flanked by large live oak trees

name: Richmond
summary: The center of Confederate manufacturing fueled a modern war, one of the South’s largest hospitals gave care to the sick and wounded, and armies battled on open fields and in miles of defensive earthworks. From 1861 to 1865, Richmond’s fate would determine America’s future.

image.caption: Cold Harbor Battlefield
image.altText: Earthen trenches running through a wooded area of bare trees and fallen autumn leaves.

name: Rio Grande
summary: For 196 miles, this free-flowing stretch of the Rio Grande winds its way through desert expanses and stunning canyons of stratified rock. For the well prepared, an extended float trip provides opportunities to explore the most remote corner of Texas and experience the ultimate in solitude, self-reliance, and immersion in natural soundscapes.

image.caption: Canoeing Boquillas Canyon
image.altText: Canoeing Boquillas Canyon

name: River Raisin
summary: River Raisin NBP preserves, commemorates, and interprets the January 1813 battles of the War of 1812 and their aftermath. Battles that resulted in the greatest victory for Tecumseh’s Confederation and the British and the greatest defeat for the U.S. The aftermath led to U.S. Indian laws that forced the removal, relocation, and assimilation of native nations, an aftermath that continues today.

image.caption: British Sled Cannon
image.altText: a sled cannon in the snow

name: Rock Creek
summary: Rock Creek Park is truly a gem in our nation's capital. This 1,754 acre city park was officially authorized in 1890, making it the third national park to be designated by the federal government. It offers visitors the opportunity to escape the bustle of the city and find a peaceful refuge, recreation, fresh air, majestic trees, wild animals, and thousands of years of human history.

image.caption: Rock Creek Park's Boulder Bridge
image.altText: Stone bridge and fall leaves

name: Rosie the Riveter WWII Home Front
summary: Celebrate and honor the contributions and sacrifices of American civilians on the WWII home front. Discover how diverse communities lived, worked, and interacted. Many faces, many stories, many truths, weave a rich tapestry of experiences from this era of opportunity and loss.

image.caption: Historic Ford Building
image.altText: Entrance sign against the historic Ford buidling.

name: Roger Williams
summary: "I acknowledge that to molest any person, Jew or Gentile, for either professing doctrine, or practicing worship meerly religious or spiritual, is to persecute him, and such a person (whether his doctrine or practice be true or false) suffers persecution for conscience." -Roger Williams, 1644 Banished by the English and saved by the First Peoples, Roger Williams founded Providence here in 1636.

image.caption: The Hahn Memorial and Crabapple Orchard
image.altText: View of the historic well through crabapple trees

name: Russell Cave
summary: Russell Cave National Monument is an archeological site with one of the most complete records of prehistoric cultures in the Southeast. In the 1950s, archeologists uncovered a large quantity of artifacts representing 12,000 years of use in a single place. Although you cannot go in the cave, the discovered artifacts help bring to light many cultural developments of phenomenal human journeys.

image.caption: Russell Cave in Spring
image.altText: Russell Cave in Spring

name: San Antonio Missions
summary: Welcome to San Antonio Missions, a National Park Service site and the only UNESCO World Heritage Site in Texas. Each mission in the park is a center of community and has been since the early 1700s. They changed life in this region, introducing new technologies while enforcing new cultural guidelines. As you visit, reflect on change, culture, power, and how people have used the land.

image.caption: Mission San Juan
image.altText: White frescoed church with a stone ruin to the left in the foreground.

name: Saint Croix
summary: Grab your paddle and your longing for adventure and head to the St. Croix and Namekagon rivers! Together they form the St. Croix National Scenic Riverway, offering over 200 miles of clean water that glides and rushes through a forested landscape. Paddle, boat, fish, and camp among this wild and scenic beauty. Hiking and historic towns also beckon.

image.caption: The St Croix River from Osceola Bluff Autumn
image.altText: A blue river winds through a valley lined with trees in autumn color.

name: Saint Croix Island
summary: The winter of 1604-1605 on Saint Croix Island was a cruel one for Pierre Dugua's French expedition. Iced in by freezing temperatures and cut off from fresh water and game, 35 of 79 men died. As spring arrived and native people traded game for bread, the health of those remaining improved. Although the expedition moved on by summer, the beginning of French presence in North America had begun.

image.caption: Saint Croix Island Entrance
image.altText: View of the drive into Saint Croix Island International Historic Site.

name: San Francisco Maritime
summary: Established in 1988, San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park celebrates America’s maritime heritage on the Pacific Coast. Our 50-acre park has grown around Aquatic Park Cove, a protected area in the stunning San Francisco Bay. As you explore the cove and the historic landmarks around it, you will experience the sights, sounds, and stories of the city’s seafaring past.

image.caption: SF Maritime NHP Fleet of Historic Ships at Mare Island.
image.altText: Five historic ships docked at Mare Island

name: Saint-Gaudens
summary: Your National Park for the Arts preserves the home and studio of sculptor Augustus Saint-Gaudens (1848-1907). Here stories flow through a landscape of inspiration. Discover the history behind the captivating bronze sculptures and enjoy the beauty of art and nature. The park and its partners continue the tradition of the Cornish Colony of artists. Unleash your creativity today.

image.caption: Amor Caritas
image.altText: gilded statue of angel with plants and reflecting pool

name: Sagamore Hill
summary: Sagamore Hill was the home of Theodore Roosevelt, 26th President of the United States, from 1885 until his death in 1919. During Roosevelt's time in office, his "Summer White House" was the focus of international attention. Explore 83 acres of natural surroundings, historic buildings and trails to become inspired by the legacy of one of America's most popular presidents.

image.caption: Theodore Roosevelt Home
image.altText: A large house painted gray with green lawn and trees.

name: Saugus Iron Works
summary: In the 1600's, on the banks of the Saugus River, something extraordinary happened! Explore the place where European iron makers brought their special skills to a young Massachusetts colony. Saugus Iron Works is a twelve-acre National Historic Site that includes working waterwheels, forges, mills, a historic 17th century home, and a lush river basin.

image.caption: Saugus Iron Works Landscape
image.altText: Several wooden structures amid green fields and trees under partly cloudy sky and beside river.

name: San Juan Island
summary: San Juan Island is well known for its splendid vistas, saltwater shores, quiet woodlands, orca whales and one of the last remaining native prairies in the Puget Sound/Northern Straits region. But it was also here in 1859 that the United States and Great Britain nearly went to war over possession of the island, the crisis ignited by the death of a pig.

image.caption: Sunset at American Camp
image.altText: a sun setting behind historic parade grounds

name: San Juan
summary: San Juan National Historic Site preserves stories of great ambition and aspirations. Countries fought for control of this tiny yet strategic island for centuries. Generations of soldiers have lived and worked within the forts. Visitors today are as inspired by these stories as they are by the beauty of the architecture and the ingenuity of design and engineering of this World Heritage Site.

name: Salem Maritime
summary: Originally established in 1938 as the first National Historic Site in the United States, Salem Maritime National Historical Park consists of nine acres of land and twelve historic structures along the Salem waterfront, as well as a downtown visitor center. Located in the urban setting of Salem, the park preserves and interprets over 600 years of New England's maritime history and global stories.

image.caption: Friendship of Salem
image.altText: A three mast tall ship on the water under a blue sky with red brick buildings on the shore.

name: Santa Monica Mountains
summary: The Santa Monica Mountains offer easy access to surprisingly wild places. Experience the famous beaches of Malibu or explore more than 500 miles of trails. The park abounds with historical and cultural sites, from old movie ranches to Native American centers. What will you and your family discover?

image.caption: Point Mugu Sunset
image.altText: Sunbeams reaching from glowing sun over the ocean.

name: Sand Creek Massacre
summary: On November 29th, 1864, Chiefs Black Kettle, White Antelope, Left Hand and others were encamped with around 750 Arapaho and Cheyenne people in a valley by the Big Sandy Creek. A hope for peace, brought forth by Black Kettle was in the balance. It was a tragic day where the blood of the Cheyenne and Arapaho was shed, and a painful memory for generations of Native Americans was made.

image.caption: Cheyenne Lodges at Dawn
image.altText: Four white Indian lodges on a grassy plain.

name: Saint Paul's Church
summary: Since 1665, Saint Paul's Church played a vital role in the colonial life of Eastchester, 20 miles north of New York City. Townspeople voted at the nearby Village Green; local militia drilled outside its doors. But the American Revolution changed everything. American, British and Hessian troops tore down the old wooden meetinghouse for firewood and used the unfinished stone chapel as a hospital.

image.caption: Rebecca Turner gravesite
image.altText: Rebecca Turner gravesite

name: Salinas Pueblo Missions
summary: Tucked away in the middle of New Mexico you’ll find Salinas Pueblo Missions National Monument. Its three distinct sites offer a glimpse into a unique time in history—a time entrenched with cultural borrowing, conflict and struggles. These sites continue to stand as reminders of the Spanish and Pueblo peoples’ early encounters and prompt exploration of today’s interactions among different people.

image.caption: Quarai Mission In Spring
image.altText: Pink flowers and green foliage frame the roofless remains of a stone mission.

name: Saratoga
summary: In 1777, a large British invasion force met an equally large American army here at Saratoga. After two intense battles, an eight-mile retreat, and a three-day siege, British General John Burgoyne surrendered his entire force. This first ever surrender of a British Army is one of the pivotal moments in determining the outcome of the Revolutionary War, forever changing the future of the world.

image.caption: John Neilson House
image.altText: A man wearing 18th-century clothing carrying a musket and a farmhouse are silhouetted by sunrise.

name: Salt River Bay
designation: National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve
summary: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve uniquely documents the human and natural Caribbean world from the earliest indigenous settlements in the central Caribbean to their clash with seven different colonial European powers to the present day.

image.caption: Salt River Bay Visitor Contact Station
image.altText: View of the Salt River Bay Visitor Contact Station

name: Scotts Bluff
summary: Towering 800 feet above the North Platte River, Scotts Bluff has served as a landmark for peoples from Native Americans to emigrants on the Oregon, California and Mormon Trails to modern travelers. Rich with geological and paleontological history as well as human history, there is much to discover while exploring the 3,000 acres of Scotts Bluff National Monument.

image.caption: Eagle Rock with Conestoga Wagon
image.altText: Conestoga wagon in front of Eagle Rock

name: Shiloh
summary: Visit the sites of the most epic struggle in the Western Theater of the Civil War. Nearly 110,000 American troops clashed in a bloody contest that resulted in 23,746 casualties; more casualties than in all of America's previous wars combined. Explore both the Shiloh and Corinth battlefields to discover the impact of this struggle on the soldiers and on the nation.

image.caption: Ruggles Battery
image.altText: Ruggles Battery at Shiloh

name: Sitka
summary: On an island amid towering spruce and hemlock, Sitka National Historical Park preserves the site of a battle between invading Russian traders and Indigenous Kiks.ádi Tlingit. Totem poles from Tlingit and Haida areas line the park’s scenic coastal trail, and the restored Russian Bishop’s House is a rare reminder of Russia’s colonial legacy in North America.

image.caption: Sunset at Sitka
image.altText: A totem pole in the foreground with a sunset over water in the background.

name: Sleeping Bear Dunes
summary: Miles of sand beach, bluffs that tower 450’ above Lake Michigan, lush forests, clear inland lakes, unique flora and fauna make up the natural world of Sleeping Bear Dunes. High dunes afford spectacular views across the lake. An island lighthouse, US Life-Saving Service stations, coastal villages, and picturesque farmsteads reflect the park’s rich maritime, agricultural, and recreational history.

image.caption: Lake Michigan overlook sun
image.altText: A bright sun begins to set into Lake Michigan

name: Springfield Armory
summary: For nearly two centuries, the U.S. Armed Forces and American industry looked to Springfield Armory for innovative engineering and superior firearms. Springfield Armory National Historic Site commemorates the critical role of the nation’s first armory by preserving and interpreting the world's largest historic US military small arms collection, along with historic archives, buildings and landscape.

image.caption: Springfield Armory National Historic Site
image.altText: The Main Arsenal

name: Springfield 1908 Race Riot
summary: In August 1908, a large White mob attacked the Black community in Springfield, Illinois. Rioters destroyed homes and businesses and lynched two men. The event led to the founding of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). Today, archeological evidence gives a rare glimpse into a community devastated by the race riots of the early 20th century.

image.caption: View of the Park Today
image.altText: A narrow grassy lot surrounded by fence.

name: Steamtown
summary: Feel the heat from the firebox, smell hot steam and oil; hear the whistle and the "chuff-chuff" from the smokestack, feel the ground vibrate, and watch as one-ton drive rods turn steel wheels. Discover how steam railroading helped shaped our nation's history and culture. Learn about the stories of the people who built, repaired and rode, and about the ongoing work to preserve railroading history.

image.caption: 6039 on the turntable
image.altText: large black train with number 6039 painted in white lettering, sitting on turntable track

name: Ste. Geneviève
summary: Established by 1750, Ste. Geneviève was the first permanent European settlement in Missouri. Early French Canadian settlers were drawn here by the rich agricultural land known as Le Grand Champ (the Big Field). After the flood of 1785, the town relocated to its present location on higher ground approximately three miles to the northwest of its original site.

image.caption: Beauvais-Amoureux House
image.altText: Frame house made of wood with U.S. and French flags flying on front porch.

name: Statue Of Liberty
summary: A gift of friendship from the people of France to the United States "The Statue of Liberty Enlightening the World" is recognized as a universal symbol of freedom and democracy. It was dedicated by President Grover Cleveland on October 28, 1886. Designated as a National Monument in 1924, employees of the National Park Service have been caring for the Statue of Liberty since 1933.

image.caption: The Statue of Liberty on Liberty Island from Statue Cruises Ferry
image.altText: Patina green statue atop her pedestal on Liberty Island; grey cloudy sky in the distance

name: Stonewall
summary: Before the 1960s, almost everything about living authentically as a lesbian, a bisexual person or a gay man was illegal. The Stonewall Uprising on June 28, 1969 is a milestone in the quest for civil rights and provided momentum for a movement.

image.caption: Tulips in Christopher Park
image.altText: Pink, purple and white tulips blooming in a park

name: Stones River
summary: The Battle of Stones River began on the last day of 1862 and became one of the bloodiest conflicts of the Civil War. The battle produced important military and political gains for the Union, and it changed forever the people who lived and fought here.

image.caption: Sunrise at Mendenhall's Artillery Trail
image.altText: The sun rises behind a green field with a cannon in the foreground.

name: Sunset Crater Volcano
summary: The lava flow lies on the land like a dream, a wonderland of rock. A thousand years ago the ground was torn open and lava erupted into the sky, forever changing the landscape and the lives of the people who lived here. A thousand years later, trees and flowers grow among the rocks, and people visit the lava flow to see and remember the most recent volcanic eruption in Arizona.

image.caption: Sunset Crater Volcano
image.altText: a cinder cone volcano and ponderosa pine trees

name: Tallgrass Prairie
summary: Tallgrass prairie once covered 170 million acres of North America, but within a generation most of it had been transformed into farms, cities, and towns. Today less than 4% remains intact, mostly in the Kansas Flint Hills. Established on November 12, 1996, the preserve protects a nationally significant remnant of the once vast tallgrass prairie ecosystem. Here the tallgrass makes its last stand.

image.caption: Fall wildflowers at the preserve
image.altText: fall wildflowers at the preserve

name: Thomas Cole
summary: In 1825, America was still a new nation, just forming its own unique identity and traditions. Thomas Cole invented a new style of art, one that Americans could call their own. His landscape paintings launched the art movement known as the Hudson River School. His groundbreaking achievements took place here in Catskill, New York -- in the "peaceful shades" of his beloved home, Cedar Grove.

name: Theodore Roosevelt Island
summary: In the 1930s, landscape architects transformed Mason’s Island from neglected, overgrown farmland into Theodore Roosevelt Island, a memorial to America’s 26th president. They conceived a “real forest” designed to mimic the natural forest that once covered the island. Today miles of trails through wooded uplands and swampy bottomlands honor the legacy of a great outdoorsman and conservationist.

image.caption: Staute of Theodore Roosevelt
image.altText: A bronze statue of Theodore Roosevelt standing and pointing.

name: Thomas Jefferson Memorial
summary: Author of the Declaration of Independence, statesman and visionary for the founding of a nation.

image.caption: Thomas Jefferson Memorial
image.altText: The Thomas Jefferson Memorial with flowering trees in the foreground

name: Thaddeus Kosciuszko
summary: Visit the house where wounded Polish freedom fighter Thaddeus Kosciuszko lived and hear how this brilliant military engineer designed successful fortifications during the American Revolution. See the room where he received notable visitors such as Chief Little Turtle and Thomas Jefferson.

image.caption: Kosciuszko House, exterior
image.altText: Color photo showing a three story brick rowhouse on a corner lot.

name: Theodore Roosevelt Birthplace
summary: This is the boyhood home of the first U.S. president to be born in New York City. Raised in a townhouse at 28 E. 20th St., Theodore Roosevelt would grow up to be our 26th President and become immortalized on Mount Rushmore. However, he started life as a sickly yet bright boy who exercised to improve his health and began a lifelong passion for the "strenuous life."

name: Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural
summary: As president, Theodore Roosevelt created protections for ordinary citizens, began regulation of big business, and made the US a major force in international affairs. Yet one of the most important presidencies in America's history nearly didn't happen. See the place where a brief, emotional, and improvised ceremony in Buffalo, NY brought TR into office, and forever altered the nation.

name: Thomas Stone
summary: In 1776, Thomas Stone and 55 others signed the Declaration of Independence. In doing so, Stone risked his home, his family's security, and even his life to support the Declaration of Independence's promise of freedom.

image.caption: Mansion at Haberdeventure
image.altText: 5 part Mansion at Haberdeventure

name: Timpanogos Cave
summary: The visitor center, caves, and cave tours have not yet opened for the 2026 season. Hike your way past stunning vistas to explore a hidden underground world. Taste the thrill of caving as you twist and bend to enter beautifully decorated rooms. Learn the science behind formations and hear stories of cave exploration and preservation. Experience and discover as you go – geologic mysteries await

image.caption: Helictites in Timpanogos Cave
image.altText: Twisty helictites growing off a stalactite

image.caption: Graball Landing
image.altText: a muddy river with trees on both sides of the riverbank

name: Timucuan
summary: Visit one of the last unspoiled coastal wetlands on the Atlantic Coast. Discover 6,000 years of human history and experience the beauty of salt marshes, coastal dunes, and hardwood hammocks. The Timucuan Preserve includes Fort Caroline and Kingsley Plantation.

image.caption: Kingsley Plantation Slave Quarters
image.altText: slave cabins made of tabby with wooden roofs

name: Tonto
summary: Located within the northern range of the Sonoran Desert lie two cliff dwellings that were occupied from 1300-1450 CE (common era). They represent a vibrant culture consisting of local and immigrant groups that lived in the Tonto Basin. Together they formed a new ideology, which archeologists refer to as Salado. Today, descendants of the cliff dwellers continue to call Arizona home.

image.caption: Lower Cliff Dwelling
image.altText: cliff dwelling in the spring with desert plants and wildflowers.

name: Touro Synagogue
summary: Touro Synagogue, a building of exquisite beauty and design, steeped in history and ideals, and one of the most historically significant Jewish buildings in America, was designated a National Historic Site in 1946. Dedicated in 1763, it still serves an active congregation and each year greets over 30,000 visitors who come to see the magnificent interior and hear its remarkable story.

name: Tuskegee Airmen
summary: Before the first African American military pilots became known as the "Red Tails" they wore striped tails as they began their flight training in the Army's PT-17 Stearman bi-plane. Their flying adventure started at Moton Field, in Tuskegee, Alabama, where the Army Air Corps conducted a military test to determine if African Americans could be trained to fly combat aircraft.

image.caption: The "Duchess Arlene" - flown by Robert Williams, Pilot class
image.altText: Red-Tail P-51D Mustang In Flight Exhibit

name: Tuskegee Institute
summary: In 1881, Booker T. Washington arrived in Alabama and started building Tuskegee Institute both in reputation and literally brick by brick. He recruited the best and the brightest to come and teach here including George Washington Carver who arrived in 1896. Carver’s innovations in agriculture, especially with peanuts, expanded Tuskegee’s standing throughout the country. The story continues….

image.caption: The Oaks - The Home of Booker T. Washington
image.altText: A three story Queen Anne Revival style red brick house

name: Tule Lake
summary: Tule Lake National Monument includes both Tule Lake Segregation Center, the largest and most controversial of the sites where Japanese Americans were incarcerated during World War II, and Camp Tulelake, which was first a Civilian Conservation Corps camp, then an additional facility to detain Japanese Americans, and finally a prisoner of war camp.

image.caption: Tule Lake National Monument Visitor Center
image.altText: White house with a concrete deck and flag poll in the front.

name: Tumacácori
summary: Tumacácori sits at a cultural crossroads in the Santa Cruz River valley. Here O’odham, Yaqui, and Apache people met and mingled with European Jesuit and Franciscan missionaries, settlers, and soldiers, sometimes in conflict and sometimes in cooperation. Follow the timeworn paths and discover stories that connect us to enduring relationships, vibrant cultures, and traditions of long ago.

image.caption: Tumacácori on a Summer Day
image.altText: panorama of mission church with green grass and clouds

name: Tupelo
summary: In July, 1864, federal forces, including men from the United States Colored Troops, marched into Tupelo, Mississippi. Disorganized Confederate soldiers fought fiercely but could not overpower the federal troops. Neither side could claim a clear victory, but Union troops had succeeded in their main goal: keeping the Confederates away from Union railroads in Tennessee.

image.caption: Tupelo National Battlefield Monument
image.altText: The monument with a cannon

name: Tule Springs Fossil Beds
summary: Over the last ~570,000 years, water has transformed the Upper Las Vegas Valley. Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument is an urban park that preserves the unique story of this ever-changing environment.

image.caption: Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument
image.altText: Tule Springs during winter

name: Tuzigoot
summary: Water flows under and through this landscape, feeding the growth of people and towns. The Verde Valley is watered by snowmelt, summer monsoons, and springs that well up from the ancient sedimentary rocks. In the heart of the valley, a thousand years ago, people began to build a little hilltop pueblo that would grow into one of the largest villages in the area.

image.caption: Tuzigoot with Tavasci Marsh
image.altText: A marsh with open water, cattails, and a masonry dwelling beyond.

name: Ulysses S Grant
summary: Ulysses S. Grant is known as the victorious Civil War general who saved the Union and the 18th President of the United States. He first met Julia Dent, his future wife, at her family home, named White Haven. From 1854 to 1859 the Dents, Grants and an enslaved African-American workforce lived on the property.

image.caption: Winter at White Haven
image.altText: Historic green house with snow on ground

name: Upper Delaware
summary: Canoe through rapids and quiet pools as the Delaware River winds its way through a valley of swiftly changing scenery or fish amid rolling hills and riverfront villages in one of the finest fishing rivers in the northeastern United States. The clean water of the Delaware, the last major undammed river in the eastern United States, supports a healthy ecosystem and offers tranquility and excitement.

image.caption: Upper Delaware Scenic and Recreational River
image.altText: a view of the Delaware River

name: Valley Forge
summary: Valley Forge is the place where George Washington and the Continental Army took refuge during the winter of 1777-1778. Today the park protects 3,500 acres of meadows, woodlands, historic landscapes, and monuments commemorating the resolve of the Revolutionary War generation and honoring the power of people to pull together, overcome adversity, and find renewal through transformation.

image.caption: Baron von Steuben Statue and Bunting
image.altText: bronze statue of rev war general on stone base, red white and blue bunting behind

name: Valles Caldera
summary: About 1.2 million years ago, a spectacular volcanic eruption created a 14-mile-wide circular depression in the earth now known as Valles Caldera. The preserve is known for its huge mountain meadows, abundant wildlife, and meandering streams. The area also preserves the homeland of ancestral native peoples and embraces a rich ranching history.

image.caption: Wide Open Views of Valles Caldera
image.altText: Scattered clouds over landscape view of winding river and brown grasslands

name: Pearl Harbor
summary: At Pearl Harbor National Memorial, we honor the lives affected by the December 7, 1941, attack. This pivotal moment in global history marked the United States' entry into World War II, impacting nations and communities worldwide. Join us in reflecting on this shared history and its lasting significance in the pursuit of peace.

image.caption: Pearl Harbor Visitor Center
image.altText: An evening photo of the Pearl Harbor Visitor Center Complex looking towards the museums.

name: Vanderbilt Mansion
summary: Built by of one of the first families of wealth in America. Designed by one of the nation's preeminent architects. The Vanderbilt Mansion is a home built expressly for the aristocratic lifestyle.

image.caption: Vanderbilt Mansion National Historic Site
image.altText: Misty April Morning

name: Vicksburg
summary: To Confederate President Jefferson Davis, Vicksburg was the "nailhead that holds the South's two halves together." President Abraham Lincoln remarked "Vicksburg is the key" to victory, and could be the north's lifeline into the south. As the federals closed in on the Fortress City, they were met by a ring of forts with over 170 cannon. The resulting battle would determine the war's outcome.

image.caption: Union Cannon
image.altText: Union cannon aimed at Confederate lines

name: Virgin Islands Coral Reef
summary: Virgin Islands Coral Reef National Monument includes federal submerged lands within the 3-mile belt off the island of St. John. These waters support a diverse and complex system of coral reefs and other ecosystems such as shoreline mangrove forests and seagrass beds.

name: Vietnam Veterans Memorial
summary: Honoring the men and women who served in the controversial Vietnam War, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial chronologically lists the names of 58,318 Americans who gave their lives in service to their country.

image.caption: Vietnam Veterans Memorial at night
image.altText: Lights glow at the base of the wall of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial with Washington Monument.

name: Washita Battlefield
summary: On November 27, 1868, Lt. Colonel George Armstrong Custer led the 7th US Cavalry on a surprise dawn attack on a Cheyenne village led by Peace Chief Black Kettle. The event was an example of the tragic clash of cultures that occurred during the Great Plains Wars. It is also a place of remembrance and reflection for those who died here. Read More

image.caption: Tipis at Sunset
image.altText: Cheyenne tipis backlite by sunset

name: Walnut Canyon
summary: Since time immemorial, Indigenous Peoples have lived and traveled throughout Walnut Canyon’s dynamic landscape. Vibrant communities built their homes in the cliffs and farmed along the canyon’s rim. Today the park preserves this landscape, and the ancestral homes in and around the canyon.

image.caption: Walnut Canyon, cliff dwellings, and the San Francisco Peaks
image.altText: Walnut Canyon's cliff dwellings are illuminated by the afternoon sun.

name: Waco Mammoth
summary: Standing as tall as 14 feet and weighing 20,000 pounds, Columbian mammoths roamed across what is present-day Texas thousands of years ago. Today, the fossil specimens represent the nation's first and only recorded evidence of a nursery herd of ice age Columbian mammoths.

image.caption: Interior of Dig Shelter
image.altText: Visitors view fossils from walkway

name: Washington Monument
summary: Built to honor George Washington, the United States' first president, the 555-foot marble obelisk towers over Washington, D.C.

image.caption: Washington Monument at Dusk
image.altText: Washington Monument at Dusk

name: War In The Pacific
summary: War in the Pacific National Historical Park was established to commemorate the bravery and sacrifice of those participating in the campaigns of the Pacific Theater of World War II and to conserve and interpret outstanding natural, scenic, and historic values and objects of the island of Guam.

image.caption: Asan Beach Overlook
image.altText: Mountain view down toward beach.

name: Weir Farm
summary: Visit the home and studio of America's most beloved Impressionist, J. Alden Weir, and walk in the footsteps of generations of world-class artists. Set amidst more than 60 acres of painterly woods, fields, and waterways, you’ll soon see why Weir described his home as the "Great Good Place." Weir’s farm is a national legacy to American Impressionism, the creative spirit, and historic preservation.

image.caption: Weir House
image.altText: A view of the south side of the Weir House with porch visable, showing a fence in front of the home

name: The White House and President's Park
summary: The White House is owned by the American people and stewarded by the National Park Service. It is more than the President's residence; it is a site for protests and national discourse about what it means to be American. As one of the most iconic sites in the country, the White House and President's Park seeks to tell the stories of all people who have lived, worked, and visited.

image.caption: White House Spring Garden Tour 2026
image.altText: Crowds of people populate the White House South Lawn on a sunny day with the White House in view

name: Whiskeytown
summary: Whiskeytown Lake’s crystal-clear waters are iconic, but this 42,000-acre National Recreation Area offers much more. Explore waterfalls, hike rugged trails, uncover Gold Rush history, and witness the resilience of nature in its post-fire recovery. Adventure awaits at every turn—Whiskeytown is calling!

image.caption: Whiskeytown Lake with the park's tallest mountains in the clouds.
image.altText: Blue-gray waters of lake with green shrub in foreground, mountains and clouds in background.

name: Whitman Mission
summary: One moment can change the fate of many nations. After thousands of years of habitation by the Cayuse Nation, life in the Columbia River Plateau begins to change rapidly with the influx of missionaries, newcomers from the Oregon Trail, and diseases. A single violent act of desperation to protect a community ignites a series of events that will reshape the United States forever.

image.caption: Tipi
image.altText: A tipi sits beneath a tree near a walking trail

name: President William Jefferson Clinton Birthplace Home
summary: Named for the father who died shortly before his birth, William Jefferson Blythe III later became the 42nd President of the United States. In Hope, the experiences shared with his mother and grandparents in rural Arkansas developed the broad views on race relations, social justice, and public service that defined his presidency and life after the White House. For Bill Clinton, "Hope was home."

image.caption: Birthplace Home
image.altText: The birthplace home of President Bill Clinton illuminated at dusk.

name: Wilson's Creek
summary: Wilson's Creek was the first major Civil War battle fought west of the Mississippi River, and where the first Union general was killed in action. The costly Southern victory on August 10, 1861, focused national attention on the war in Missouri. Wilson’s Creek National Battlefield commemorates and interprets the battle within the context of the war in the Trans-Mississippi West.

image.caption: Edwards Cabin
image.altText: Women in reproduction historic dress sit and stand on porch of old cabin

name: William Howard Taft
summary: High atop one of Cincinnati's most prominent hilltops stands the two-story Greek Revival house where William Howard Taft was born and grew up. Hard work, a good education, and an interest in civic duty are attributes that made the Taft family outstanding leaders over the years. The environment that shaped Taft's character and philosophy is highlighted on a visit to the site.

image.caption: The Taft Family Home in Summer
image.altText: A yellow two-story brick building with tall windows and green shutters on them

name: Women's Rights
summary: Women’s Rights National Historical Park tells the story of the first Women’s Rights Convention, held in Seneca Falls, New York on July 19-20, 1848. It is a story of struggles for civil rights, human rights, and equality, global struggles that continue today. The efforts of women’s rights leaders, abolitionists, and other 19th century reformers remind us that all people must be accepted as equals.

image.caption: Wesleyan Chapel
image.altText: The Wesleyan Chapel in summer

name: Wolf Trap National Park for the Performing Arts
summary: No matter what your age or taste in shows, you'll find something you like onstage at Wolf Trap National Park for the Performing Arts. From May through September, multiple amphitheaters in the park present performances such as musicals, dance, opera, jazz, and popular and country music. A good time to explore the beauty and history of the park without the crowds is October - April.

image.caption: Filene Center Blast Off
image.altText: The Filene Center House full of patrons

name: Wright Brothers
summary: Wind, sand, and a dream of flight brought Wilbur and Orville Wright to Kitty Hawk, North Carolina where, after four years of scientific experimentation, they achieved the first successful airplane flights on December 17, 1903. With courage and perseverance, these self-taught engineers relied on teamwork and application of the scientific process. What they achieved changed our world forever.

image.caption: Busts and Moon
image.altText: Copper busts of the two brothers with the moon visible in the blue sky.

name: Wupatki
summary: Nestled between the Painted Desert and ponderosa highlands of northern Arizona, Wupatki National Monument is an unlikely landscape for a thriving community. The early 1100's marked a time of cooler and wetter weather, when the ancestors of contemporary Pueblo communities created a bustling center of trade and culture. For indigenous peoples, these sites represent the footprints of their ancestors.

image.caption: Wupatki Pueblo
image.altText: a large stone pueblo in a desert beneath mostly sunny skies with mountains in background

name: World War II Memorial
summary: Through stone architecture and bronze sculptures, the World War II Memorial recognizes the ways Americans served, honors those who fell, and recognizes the victory they achieved to restore freedom and end tyranny around the globe.

image.caption: A Field of Stars
image.altText: Close up of Gold Stars in the Memorial

name: World War I Memorial
summary: A grateful nation honors the service, valor, courage and sacrifice of the 4.7 million American sons and daughters who served in the Great War.

image.caption: General Pershing Statue
image.altText: General Pershing Statue

name: Yorktown Battlefield
designation: Part of Colonial National Historical Park
summary: Discover what it took for the United States to be independent as you explore the site of the last major battle of the Revolutionary War. Here at Yorktown, in the fall of 1781, General George Washington, with allied American and French forces, besieged General Charles Lord Cornwallis’s British army. On October 19, Cornwallis surrendered, effectively ending the war and ensuring independence.

image.caption: Cannon at Sunset Yorktown Battlefield
image.altText: Cannon at sunset at Yorktown Battlefield

name: Yukon - Charley Rivers
summary: Located in Interior Alaska, Yukon-Charley Rivers offers exploration in a largely untouched landscape. Whether you float the mighty Yukon River or paddle the Charley River's whitewater, your memories will last a lifetime. Geology, cultural history, gold rush remnants, wildlife, and vast scenery will be a part of your experience. But, the strongest element will be solitude. Your adventure awaits.

image.caption: Aerial view of the Yukon River
image.altText: Aerial view of the Yukon River during fall colors

name: Yucca House
summary: Yucca House National Monument preserves a large unexcavated pueblo with a stunning setting in Montezuma Valley, nestled between Mesa Verde and Ute Mountain. Since Yucca House was protected as a national monument in 1919, it has remained largely untouched, offering intrepid visitors a sense of discovery and preserving the pueblo's beauty and integrity for future generations.

image.caption: Yucca House Spring
image.altText: Cattails with mesa in background.

name: Anza-Borrego Desert
summary: California's largest state park: badlands, palm oases, slot canyons and wildflower springs in the Colorado Desert east of San Diego. Named for the explorer Juan Bautista de Anza and the borrego, the desert bighorn sheep.

image.credit: No machine-readable author provided. Miskatonic assumed (based on copyright claims)., via Wikimedia Commons

name: Big Basin Redwoods
summary: California's oldest state park, in the Santa Cruz Mountains — a bowl of old-growth coast redwoods draining down Waddell Creek to the sea. Much of the forest burned in 2020 and is regrowing.

name: Julia Pfeiffer Burns
summary: A stretch of the Big Sur coast where McWay Falls drops 80 feet from a cliff onto a cove beach, with redwood canyons inland. Named for a pioneer rancher of Big Sur.

name: Humboldt Redwoods
summary: Home of Rockefeller Forest, the largest remaining old-growth coast redwood forest in the world, along the Eel River in northern California. The Avenue of the Giants runs through it.

name: Point Lobos
summary: A granite headland south of Carmel where cypress groves, coves and tide pools meet one of the richest marine habitats in California. Sea otters, seals and, in season, grey whales are often seen offshore.

name: Mount Tamalpais
summary: The 2,571-foot mountain rising above Marin County, with redwood canyons, oak woodland and views over San Francisco Bay from its summit. It surrounds Muir Woods National Monument.

image.credit: Oscar Vasquez / California Department of Parks and Recreation, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Emerald Bay
summary: One of Lake Tahoe's most photographed bays, with Fannette Island — the lake's only island — Eagle Falls, and Vikingsholm, a 38-room mansion in Scandinavian style on the shore.

name: Valley of Fire
summary: Nevada's oldest state park: red Aztec Sandstone that seems to burn in low sun, carved into arches, domes and narrow canyons, with petroglyphs left by ancient peoples. An hour northeast of Las Vegas.

name: Dead Horse Point
summary: A mesa-top overlook 2,000 feet above a gooseneck of the Colorado River, next to Canyonlands National Park near Moab. Known for sunrise views and dark night skies.

name: Goblin Valley
summary: A basin of thousands of mushroom-shaped hoodoos — the goblins — in the San Rafael Desert of central Utah, free to wander among on foot.

name: Snow Canyon
summary: A canyon of red and white Navajo Sandstone with lava flows, lava tubes and sand dunes, on the edge of St. George in southwestern Utah.

name: Kodachrome Basin
summary: Colourful sandstone and nearly 70 tall stone spires, or sand pipes, near Bryce Canyon in southern Utah, named after Kodachrome film by a National Geographic expedition.

name: Coral Pink Sand Dunes
summary: Shifting dunes of pink-orange sand below red cliffs in southern Utah, home to a beetle found nowhere else and popular for sandboarding and off-road driving.

name: Antelope Island
summary: The largest island in the Great Salt Lake, with bison, pronghorn and bighorn sheep, salt-flat beaches and huge flocks of migrating birds. Reached by a causeway from near Salt Lake City.

name: Custer
summary: South Dakota's first and largest state park, in the Black Hills: prairie and granite peaks, a large free-roaming bison herd, and the Needles Highway and Wildlife Loop Road.

name: Smith Rock
summary: Cliffs of volcanic tuff and basalt above a bend of the Crooked River in central Oregon, considered the birthplace of American sport climbing.

name: Silver Falls
summary: Oregon's largest state park, where the Trail of Ten Falls follows Silver Creek's canyon past ten waterfalls — four of which you can walk behind.

image.credit: Kelvin Kay -- Kkmd at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Deception Pass
summary: Forested islands, beaches and tidal currents around the narrow channel between Whidbey and Fidalgo Islands in Washington, spanned by the twin arches of the 1930s Deception Pass Bridge.

name: Palouse Falls
summary: A 200-foot waterfall plunging into a basalt canyon in southeast Washington's Channeled Scablands, carved by the ice-age Missoula Floods. Washington's official state waterfall.

image.credit: Bala Sivakumar from Seattle, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Chugach
summary: Nearly half a million acres of mountains, glaciers and valleys right on the eastern edge of Anchorage, one of the largest state parks in the country.

name: Denali
summary: Mountains and lakes along the Parks Highway east of Denali National Park, with some of the best views of Denali from the road on clear days.

name: Kachemak Bay
summary: Alaska's first state park: glaciers, mountains, fjords and coastline across the bay from Homer, reached only by boat or plane.

image.credit: Beeblebrox ( talk ) 06:06, 13 January 2009 (UTC), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Nā Pali Coast
summary: Sheer, fluted sea cliffs and hanging valleys along Kauaʻi's northwest shore, reached on foot only by the Kalalau Trail, or seen from boats and the air. The valleys were farmed by Hawaiians for centuries.

name: Waimea Canyon
summary: The "Grand Canyon of the Pacific": a canyon about ten miles long and up to 3,000 feet deep on Kauaʻi, cut into red volcanic rock by rivers fed from one of the wettest places on Earth.

name: Kartchner Caverns
summary: A living limestone cave in southern Arizona, discovered by two cavers in 1974 and kept secret for years to protect it. Seen only on guided tours.

name: Slide Rock
summary: A natural water slide in the slippery bed of Oak Creek, among red rocks north of Sedona, Arizona, beside a historic apple farm.

image.credit: Don Graham from Redlands, CA, USA - God bless it!, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Roxborough
summary: Tilted slabs of red sandstone jutting from the foothills south of Denver — the same rock as Red Rocks and the Garden of the Gods. A National Natural Landmark.

image.credit: Greg Willis from Denver, CO, usa, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Eldorado Canyon
summary: A narrow canyon of sheer sandstone walls south of Boulder, Colorado, and one of the country's best-known climbing areas. Timed entry is needed on summer weekends.

name: Palo Duro Canyon
summary: The second-largest canyon in the United States, cut into the Texas Panhandle in banded red and gold rock. The outdoor musical TEXAS is staged in the canyon each summer.

image.credit: Larry D. Moore, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Big Bend Ranch
summary: The largest state park in Texas: remote desert mountains, canyons and the Rio Grande along the Mexican border, west of Big Bend National Park.

image.credit: Surfsupusa at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Enchanted Rock
summary: A huge dome of pink granite in the Texas Hill Country, rising about 425 feet above the land around it. The rock creaks as it cools at night, the source of many local legends.

name: Caprock Canyons
summary: Red-rock canyons on the edge of the Llano Estacado in the Texas Panhandle, home to the official Texas State Bison Herd.

name: City of Rocks
summary: Volcanic rock formations up to 40 feet high, rising from the high desert of southwestern New Mexico like the streets of a city.

name: Bruneau Dunes
summary: Home to the tallest single-structured sand dune in North America, beside small lakes in the desert of southwestern Idaho, with an observatory for dark-sky viewing.

name: Makoshika
summary: Montana's largest state park: badlands on the edge of Glendive with fossils of dinosaurs such as Triceratops and Tyrannosaurus in the Hell Creek Formation.

image.credit: Larry D. Moore, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Hot Springs
summary: Hot springs in Thermopolis, Wyoming, that flow at 135°F over terraces of mineral deposits, with free bathing at the State Bath House and a state bison herd.

name: Itasca
summary: Minnesota's oldest state park, around Lake Itasca, where you can walk across the stones at the headwaters of the Mississippi River. Old-growth red and white pines grow along its shores.

image.credit: Mark Evans from Orange City, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Starved Rock
summary: Sandstone canyons with seasonal waterfalls along the Illinois River, Illinois's most visited state park, named for a legend of a siege on the butte above the river.

image.credit: Chris Light ( talk ), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Devil's Lake
summary: Wisconsin's largest state park: a glacial lake ringed by 500-foot quartzite bluffs in the Baraboo Range, with boulder-field trails and rock climbing, northwest of Madison.

name: Porcupine Mountains Wilderness
summary: Old-growth hardwood forest, waterfalls and the Lake of the Clouds in the Porcupine Mountains along Lake Superior, in Michigan's Upper Peninsula — one of the largest old-growth forests west of the Adirondacks.

image.credit: w:Flickr user Erik Abderhalden, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tahquamenon Falls
summary: One of the largest waterfalls east of the Mississippi, where the root-beer-coloured Tahquamenon River drops over the Upper Falls in Michigan's Upper Peninsula, with a set of smaller Lower Falls downstream.

image.credit: Dawn Endico from Menlo Park, California, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Hocking Hills
summary: Sandstone gorges, recess caves and waterfalls in southeastern Ohio, including Old Man's Cave, Ash Cave and Cedar Falls, linked by trails open all year.

name: Brown County
summary: Indiana's largest state park, in wooded hills near Nashville, known for its autumn colour and long views from its fire tower and overlooks.

name: Turkey Run
summary: Indiana's second state park: deep sandstone ravines along Sugar Creek, with ladders and narrow canyon trails, and a historic inn.

name: Cumberland Falls
summary: A 68-foot curtain of water on the Cumberland River in Kentucky, one of the few places in the Western Hemisphere where a moonbow forms regularly on clear nights at the full moon.

name: Fall Creek Falls
summary: Tennessee's largest state park, on the Cumberland Plateau, named for its 256-foot waterfall — among the highest free-falling falls in the eastern United States.

name: Cloudland Canyon
summary: A deep gorge cut into the western edge of Lookout Mountain in northwest Georgia, with rim views and two waterfalls at its foot.

image.credit: Ronmacal at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tallulah Gorge
summary: A 1,000-foot-deep gorge in northeast Georgia where the Tallulah River drops over a series of six waterfalls, with a suspension bridge across it and a floor reached by permit.

name: Providence Canyon
summary: Georgia's "Little Grand Canyon": gullies up to 150 feet deep, eroded since the 1800s from poor farming practices into soft sediments of pink, orange and purple.

name: Chimney Rock
summary: A granite spire rising above Hickory Nut Gorge near Asheville, North Carolina, with views over Lake Lure and a 404-foot waterfall nearby. Hurricane Helene in 2024 damaged the park and the village below it.

name: Jockey's Ridge
summary: The tallest active sand dune system in the eastern United States, on North Carolina's Outer Banks at Nags Head — a favourite for hang gliding and sunset walks.

image.credit: Pytheas at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Table Rock
summary: A granite mountain with a bare, flat-topped face at the edge of South Carolina's Blue Ridge, with a historic lodge and stonework built by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

name: Bahia Honda
summary: A Florida Keys island with some of the Keys' best beaches, clear water for snorkelling, and the remains of Henry Flagler's Overseas Railroad bridge.

name: John Pennekamp Coral Reef
summary: The first underwater park in the United States, off Key Largo in the Florida Keys, protecting coral reefs reached by snorkel and glass-bottom boat tours.

image.credit: Matt Kieffer from London, United Kingdom, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Ichetucknee Springs
summary: Clear, spring-fed water flowing six miles through shaded forest in north Florida, famous for summer tubing and for swimming in its springs.

name: Myakka River
summary: One of Florida's oldest and largest state parks, with wetlands, prairies and a river full of alligators and wading birds, and a canopy walkway through the treetops.

name: Petit Jean
summary: Arkansas's first state park, on a mountain above the Arkansas River: Cedar Falls, a canyon, bluffs and lodge buildings built by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

name: Ha Ha Tonka
summary: The stone ruins of an early twentieth-century castle on a bluff above the Lake of the Ozarks in Missouri, with sinkholes, a natural bridge and a large spring.

image.credit: Paul Knittel from St. Louis, United States, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Letchworth
summary: The "Grand Canyon of the East": the Genesee River runs through a gorge up to 550 feet deep and over three large waterfalls in western New York.

name: Watkins Glen
summary: A narrow gorge in New York's Finger Lakes where a stone path and stairs lead past 19 waterfalls, under and behind some of them.

image.credit: Flickr user: Peter Rivera Stamford, Connecticut https://www.flickr.com/people/riverap1/, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Niagara Falls
summary: The oldest state park in the United States, designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, on the American side of Niagara Falls with Goat Island, the American Falls and views of the Horseshoe Falls.

name: Ricketts Glen
summary: Old-growth forest and 24 named waterfalls along Kitchen Creek in northeastern Pennsylvania, many of them on the Falls Trail loop.

name: Ohiopyle
summary: Whitewater rafting and kayaking in the Youghiogheny River gorge of southwestern Pennsylvania, with waterfalls, natural water slides and the Great Allegheny Passage bike trail.

image.credit: Hubert Stoffels from Pittsburgh, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Baxter
summary: A wilderness park in north-central Maine around Katahdin, the state's highest mountain and the northern end of the Appalachian Trail, given to the state by Governor Percival Baxter.

image.credit: TJ aka Teej at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Franconia Notch
summary: A mountain pass in New Hampshire's White Mountains with the Flume Gorge, the Cannon Mountain tramway and the site of the Old Man of the Mountain, which collapsed in 2003.

name: Mount Greylock
summary: The highest point in Massachusetts, crowned by a war memorial tower, and the state's first public land set aside to protect forest.

name: Cape Henlopen
summary: Dunes, beaches and maritime forest where Delaware Bay meets the Atlantic, with Second World War observation towers and a fishing pier.

name: Blackwater Falls
summary: A 62-foot waterfall where the tea-coloured Blackwater River drops into its canyon in West Virginia's Allegheny Mountains, with a lodge on the rim.

image.credit: Tim Kiser ( w:User:Malepheasant ), via Wikimedia Commons

name: Grayson Highlands
summary: High balds, rocky outcrops and wild ponies on the slopes beside Mount Rogers in southwest Virginia, crossed by the Appalachian Trail.

image.credit: Virginia State Parks staff, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Natural Bridge
summary: A 215-foot-high limestone arch over Cedar Creek in Virginia's Shenandoah Valley, the remains of an ancient cave roof, once owned by Thomas Jefferson.

name: Fort Robinson
summary: A former US Army fort in the Pine Ridge of northwest Nebraska, where the Lakota leader Crazy Horse was killed in 1877. Bison and bighorn sheep roam the buttes.

name: Maquoketa Caves
summary: More caves than any other state park in Iowa, with a natural bridge and limestone bluffs along a wooded valley, and buildings by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

name: Robbers Cave
summary: Wooded hills and sandstone cliffs in the Sans Bois Mountains of southeast Oklahoma, with a cave said to have hidden outlaws including Belle Starr and Jesse James.

image.credit: Thomas & Dianne Jones from Okmulgee, USA, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Tishomingo
summary: Sandstone outcrops, a swinging bridge and canoe trips on Bear Creek in the Appalachian foothills of northeast Mississippi, on the Natchez Trace Parkway.

name: Gulf
summary: White-sand Gulf beaches, dunes, freshwater lakes and pine forest at Gulf Shores, Alabama, with a long fishing pier.

name: High Point
summary: The highest point in New Jersey, topped by a 220-foot war memorial obelisk, in the Kittatinny Mountains where New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania meet.

image.credit: AndyZ at en.wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Grand Staircase-Escalante
summary: Vast, remote plateau and canyon country in southern Utah — the cliffs of the Grand Staircase, the Kaiparowits Plateau and the slot canyons of the Escalante — rich in dinosaur fossils. Its boundaries have been redrawn several times by presidential proclamation, most recently in 2026.

image.credit: Bureau of Land Management (mypubliclands on Flickr) https://www.flickr.com/people/mypubliclands/, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Vermilion Cliffs
summary: Red cliffs, Paria Canyon and the swirling sandstone of Coyote Buttes, home of the Wave, on the Arizona–Utah line. Visiting the Wave needs a permit from a lottery, and California condors fly overhead.

name: Bears Ears
summary: Canyon country around a pair of buttes in southeastern Utah, with tens of thousands of cultural sites — cliff dwellings, rock art and granaries — sacred to the tribes who help manage it. Its boundaries have been redrawn by successive presidents.

name: Canyons of the Ancients
summary: The densest known concentration of archaeological sites in the United States, in southwestern Colorado: Ancestral Puebloan villages, towers and cliff dwellings, with the Anasazi Heritage Center as its museum.

image.credit: Bureau of Land Management, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks
summary: The jagged granite spires of the Organ Mountains above Las Cruces, New Mexico, and desert ranges to the west with petroglyphs and traces of the Butterfield stage route.

image.credit: Bureau of Land Management, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Kasha-Katuwe Tent Rocks
summary: Cone-shaped tent rocks of volcanic ash and pumice and a narrow slot canyon near Cochiti Pueblo, southwest of Santa Fe. The road crosses Pueblo land and the monument has been closed for long periods, so check before you go.

image.credit: VitaleBaby at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Carrizo Plain
summary: California's largest remaining native grassland, split by the San Andreas Fault, with the salt flats of Soda Lake, the rock art of Painted Rock and spring wildflower blooms.

image.credit: John Wiley User:Jw4nvc - Santa Barbara, California, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Basin and Range
summary: Remote, empty mountains and valleys in southeastern Nevada, with ancient rock art. Michael Heizer's vast land artwork City lies within it.

image.credit: U.S. Department of the Interior, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Gold Butte
summary: Red sandstone towers, rock art and desert tortoise habitat northeast of Las Vegas, with the remains of an old mining town, reached by rough roads.

image.credit: US Bureau of Land Management, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Red Rock Canyon
summary: Red and cream sandstone cliffs 15 miles west of Las Vegas, with a 13-mile scenic drive, desert hiking and world-class climbing. The scenic drive needs a timed-entry reservation for much of the year.

name: Sonoran Desert
summary: Saguaro forests and desert mountain ranges southwest of Phoenix, crossed by historic trails used by Spanish explorers, the Mormon Battalion and the Butterfield stage.

image.credit: Bureau of Land Management, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Upper Missouri River Breaks
summary: Badlands, white sandstone cliffs and 149 miles of the Missouri River in central Montana, little changed since Lewis and Clark passed in 1805 — best seen by canoe.

name: Mojave Trails
summary: Desert mountains, lava flows, sand dunes and the longest undeveloped stretch of Route 66, between Interstates 15 and 40 in California's Mojave Desert.

image.credit: Bob Wick of the Bureau of Land Management, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Mount St. Helens
summary: The volcano that erupted on May 18, 1980, and the blast zone around it, left to recover naturally, with lava tubes at Ape Cave on its south side. Managed by the US Forest Service.

name: Newberry
summary: Lava flows, a glassy obsidian flow and two lakes in the caldera of the Newberry Volcano south of Bend, Oregon, with Lava Butte and the Lava River Cave. Managed by the US Forest Service.

image.credit: Q Myers, en:User:QDM, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Misty Fjords
summary: Sheer granite fjords, waterfalls and cliffs east of Ketchikan, Alaska, almost all of it wilderness and reached by boat or floatplane. Part of the Tongass National Forest.

image.credit: Zarxos at English Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Admiralty Island
summary: Kootznoowoo, the "fortress of the bears" in Tlingit: a big, forested island near Juneau with one of the densest brown bear populations in the world. Part of the Tongass National Forest.

image.credit: Nick Bonzey from Juneau, AK, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Arctic
summary: The largest wildlife refuge in the country, in Alaska's far northeast: Brooks Range peaks, tundra and the coastal plain where the Porcupine caribou herd gives birth. Gwich'in and Iñupiat homeland, with no roads in.

image.credit: Steven Chase, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Bosque del Apache
summary: Wetlands along the Rio Grande in New Mexico where tens of thousands of sandhill cranes and snow geese spend the winter. Their flights at dawn and dusk draw crowds in November and December.

name: Okefenokee
summary: The largest blackwater swamp in North America, on the Georgia–Florida line: cypress, open prairies and floating peat islands, with alligators and sandhill cranes, explored by boat on water trails.

image.credit: US Fish and Wildlife Service, via Wikimedia Commons

name: J.N. "Ding" Darling
summary: Mangrove estuary on Sanibel Island, Florida, known for wading birds such as roseate spoonbills and for its four-mile Wildlife Drive. Named for the conservationist cartoonist Jay Norwood "Ding" Darling.

name: Chincoteague
summary: Beaches, dunes and marsh on the Virginia end of Assateague Island, home of the Chincoteague ponies and a stop for huge numbers of migrating shorebirds and waterfowl.

image.credit: Leonard J. DeFrancisci, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Malheur
summary: Lakes and marshes in Oregon's high desert, one of the most important stopovers for migrating birds in the American West.

image.credit: Oregon Department of Transportation, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Wichita Mountains
summary: Granite mountains and mixed-grass prairie in southwest Oklahoma, the oldest managed refuge in the US Fish and Wildlife Service system. Bison were restored here in 1907, and elk and Texas longhorns roam too.

name: National Elk
summary: Winter range for one of the largest elk herds in North America, on the edge of Jackson, Wyoming. In winter, horse-drawn sleighs carry visitors among thousands of elk.
